title: Foundation for Virtual and Augmented Reality Systems

course_goals.text: Analyze the foundational concepts, historical evolution, and inherent challenges of Extended Reality (XR) systems, including psychological dimensions and cultural applications.
Design and analyze the complete architecture of immersive XR systems, integrating hardware components, tracking mechanisms, and user-centric software development principles.
Evaluate the influence of human sensory perception and physiological processes on XR design, focusing on visual, auditory, and non-visual factors to enhance immersion.
Apply optimization techniques and rigorous empirical methods to enhance XR performance, mitigate physiological discomfort, and implement complex systems using industry tools.

concepts.name: XR
concepts.definition: XR stands for extended reality.

concepts.name: VR
concepts.definition: VR stands for virtual reality.

concepts.name: AR
concepts.definition: AR stands for augmented reality.

concepts.name: MR
concepts.definition: MR is another term called mixed reality.

concepts.name: headset
concepts.definition: It is worn on the head, blocks our vision, and transports us to a virtual world which we can experience through the headset.

concepts.name: Immersive technologies
concepts.definition: These are technologies where the user experiences an environment through sensory organs in a way that makes them fail to distinguish it from reality.

concepts.name: Immersive
concepts.definition: It describes a perceived experience through sensory organs that appears to be real, causing the user to assume the environment is real.

concepts.name: reality-virtuality continuum
concepts.definition: It is essentially referring to a scale that spans from the real environment to the virtual environment.

concepts.name: real environment
concepts.definition: This is one extreme of the scale where there is nothing virtual.

concepts.name: virtual environment
concepts.definition: This is the other extreme of the scale where there is nothing real.

concepts.name: augmented virtuality
concepts.definition: Augmented virtuality is the opposite of augmented reality, where we are augmenting the virtual world with real world content.

concepts.name: Metaverse
concepts.definition: It is a concept that reimagines how humans interact with the digital world, moving beyond flat screens into an all-around 3D environment where users interact naturally.

concepts.name: AR VR systems
concepts.definition: These are the technologies that students will learn how to develop and deploy to master the field of virtual reality and augmented reality.

concepts.name: Application areas
concepts.definition: Application areas are the different areas pertaining to extended reality that the course will cover.

concepts.name: Categories of systems
concepts.definition: Categories of systems are different types of systems viewed from the application point of view that are present in the market.

concepts.name: Use forecasts
concepts.definition: Use forecasts are predictions about the likely scenario down the line in terms of application of extended reality technology.

concepts.name: virtual tours
concepts.definition: Virtual tours are experiences that give the user the experience of visiting a place without physically going there.

concepts.name: virtual tourism
concepts.definition: Virtual tourism is a popular method that allows users to explore faraway places while saving money and physical effort.

concepts.name: heritage tourism
concepts.definition: Heritage tourism allows users to visit a heritage place virtually, enabling them to explore every part of the space without physically going there.

concepts.name: Non-immersive VR system
concepts.definition: A virtual experience obtained through a computer where the user can control characters or activities within the software, but the environment is not directly interacting with the user.

concepts.name: Augmentation of real-world content with digital content
concepts.definition: This is the focus of AR, which involves adding digital content onto real-world content.

concepts.name: Immersive experience
concepts.definition: This is a term emphasized when discussing VR, but it is not mandatory in the case of AR.

concepts.name: Reconstruction of lost structures
concepts.definition: This is an interesting application area where lost structures can be added to the screen using AR.

concepts.name: Virtual tape measure
concepts.definition: This is an augmented reality application that allows users to measure heights or lengths without needing a physical tape.

concepts.name: Customer experience
concepts.definition: This refers to providing customers with the ability to test or visualize products in their environment before making a purchase decision.

concepts.name: Telemedicine
concepts.definition: This is an option that enables medical professionals to interact with patients using AR.

concepts.name: VR system categories
concepts.definition: These three categories (non-immersive, semi-immersive, and fully immersive) are based on the importance of the psychological aspect and user experience.

concepts.name: Marker-based
concepts.definition: These systems are easier to make and rely on simple algorithms, but they are difficult to maintain unless the environment is highly sanitized.

concepts.name: Markerless
concepts.definition: These techniques are used to overcome marker maintenance issues and primarily rely on computer vision, sometimes utilizing other sensors.

concepts.name: Superimposition-based
concepts.definition: This is a type of computer vision-based application used in AR.

concepts.name: Projection-based techniques
concepts.definition: These techniques, such as holographic projection, can be utilized in AR application development.

concepts.name: Virtual
concepts.definition: Being in essence or effect but not in fact.

concepts.name: Reality
concepts.definition: The state or quality of being real, or something that exists independently of ideas concerning it.

concepts.name: Artificial environment
concepts.definition: An artificial environment is a computer-generated, synthetic graphical view of a real or imaginary world that must be populated with artificial objects.

concepts.name: Sensory stimuli
concepts.definition: Computer-generated inputs, such as sights and sounds, that allow the user to experience the artificial environment.

concepts.name: Interaction
concepts.definition: The dynamic change in the virtual environment that occurs based on the user's actions or inputs.

concepts.name: VR system
concepts.definition: A system is classified as a VR system only if it satisfies all three characteristics: virtual environment, immersive experience, and interaction.

concepts.name: Characteristics of AR system
concepts.definition: The defining features of an AR system, which include combining real with virtual, being interactive in real time, being registered in 3D, and being experienced through sensory organs.

concepts.name: Overlay digital information
concepts.definition: The process of placing digital information onto a representation of reality or an image of reality that is being viewed through a device.

concepts.name: Registered in 3D
concepts.definition: The requirement that digital content appears at the appropriate place when enhancing reality, allowing for seamless mixing with real-world objects.

concepts.name: Augmented reality system
concepts.definition: AR systems are the ones which augment or enhance our sense of reality.

concepts.name: Formative years
concepts.definition: This phase is roughly associated with the years between 1950 and 1990.

concepts.name: Modern phase
concepts.definition: This phase is defined as the period between 1991 and 2015.

concepts.name: Growth phase
concepts.definition: This is the current phase, which roughly started from 2016 onwards.

concepts.name: Stereoscopic device
concepts.definition: A stereoscopic device is a tool used to demonstrate that the brain can process two-dimensional images as three-dimensional objects.

concepts.name: Immersion
concepts.definition: Immersion is the state where 2D images are perceived as 3D objects or 3D space due to stereoscopic vision.

concepts.name: Stereoscope
concepts.definition: A stereoscope is a compact-sized device created to generate the illusion of depth when viewing images.

concepts.name: Flight simulator
concepts.definition: A flight simulator is a concept, first introduced in 1928, that utilizes multiple sensors to provide an immersive experience.

concepts.name: HMDs or head-mounted displays
concepts.definition: A new kind of computer display that people started working on in the 1950s.

concepts.name: Sensorama
concepts.definition: A device that tried to engage all our sensory organs, and is considered the first immersive virtual reality system.

concepts.name: Haptic feedback
concepts.definition: A sensation that allows the user to feel objects on the screen through touch.

concepts.name: Virtual Visual Environment Display
concepts.definition: The first commercially viable stereoscopic head-tracked HMD with a wide field of view.

concepts.name: CAVE system
concepts.definition: A system that renders images in a surrounding setting, giving an immersive experience.

concepts.name: WTK package
concepts.definition: A software package developed for higher level application development in VR.

concepts.name: VRML
concepts.definition: A virtual reality modeling language.

concepts.name: White 5
concepts.definition: A 150-degree FOV field of view HMD.

concepts.name: Oculus Rift
concepts.definition: An inexpensive VR headset created in 2012.

concepts.name: commercial VR headsets
concepts.definition: These are well-known company releases starting around 2016 that made immersive experiences affordable to a large population, thereby spurring growth in the field.

concepts.name: Experimental phase
concepts.definition: This phase, which happened before the 1980s, was primarily related to early experimentation, defining concepts and showing different types of required technology.

concepts.name: Basic research phase
concepts.definition: This phase, occurring between the 1980s and mid-1990s, involved research into enabling technologies such as tracking, displays, and input devices.

concepts.name: Tools or applications phase
concepts.definition: During this phase, which ran from the mid-1990s to 2007, early applications and exploratory tasks related to interaction techniques and design theory were developed.

concepts.name: Commercial application phase
concepts.definition: The commercial application phase, which began in 2007 and continues to date, is marked by widespread AR availability and the continuous emergence of newer applications in the market.

concepts.name: Tracking
concepts.definition: Tracking technology is used to register content in 3D.

concepts.name: Optical see-through head mounted display
concepts.definition: This is a CRT-based display that allows the user to see through it while wearing it.

concepts.name: Computer-generated imagery
concepts.definition: This is imagery created by a computer that can be superimposed over the real world view or used as a substitute for the real world.

concepts.name: Super cockpit program
concepts.definition: This was a major program of the US Air Force that resulted in many relevant technologies for augmented reality.

concepts.name: AR-type applications
concepts.definition: These are precursors to the type of AR applications that are seen nowadays.

concepts.name: Wearable computers
concepts.definition: Wearable computers are setups where a headset is worn and the computer is carried in a backpack, utilizing various input devices.

concepts.name: AR overlay on real-world markers
concepts.definition: This involves using computer vision techniques to place augmented reality content onto real-world markers.

concepts.name: Viewpoint tracking
concepts.definition: Viewpoint tracking is the activity addressing the challenge of accurately tracking how the user's viewpoint is registered in 3D.

concepts.name: AR Toolkit tracking library
concepts.definition: This library provided real-time computer vision based tracking of a square marker.

concepts.name: Mobile phone based AR application
concepts.definition: This refers to the first demonstration of an augmented reality application utilizing a mobile phone.

concepts.name: Commercial phase
concepts.definition: The commercial phase is characterized by AR experiences starting to become very popular.

concepts.name: ARKit SDK
concepts.definition: This is the SDK launched by Apple in 2017 for AR system development.

concepts.name: ARCore
concepts.definition: ARCore is a technology released by Google for Android OS or Android platforms.

concepts.name: Commercial growth phase
concepts.definition: The commercial growth phase is characterized by the expectation that more applications and tools will become available as time passes, leading to continued growth.

concepts.name: Issues and challenges
concepts.definition: These are the problems and difficulties that exist within virtual and augmented reality systems.

concepts.name: Synonyms
concepts.definition: The terms augmented reality and mixed reality are used interchangeably and are considered synonyms.

concepts.name: Virtual reality system
concepts.definition: An artificial environment which is experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, in which one's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.

concepts.name: Objective of any VR system
concepts.definition: To let the user experience an artificial environment through sensory stimuli provided by the computer.

concepts.name: Technological issue
concepts.definition: The challenge of how to generate suitable stimuli to experience the virtual or artificial environment.

concepts.name: Psychological issue
concepts.definition: The challenge of how the user perceives the generated stimuli, which relates to the role of the human factor and psychological characteristics.

concepts.name: Immersion
concepts.definition: Immersion is the objective degree to which a VR system and application projects stimuli onto the sensory receptors of users in a way that is extensive, matching, surrounding, vivid, interactive and plot informing.

concepts.name: Extensive
concepts.definition: Extensive refers to the range of sensory modalities that are presented to the user.

concepts.name: Matching
concepts.definition: Matching refers to the congruence between sensory modalities, such as appropriate visual presentation corresponding to head motion.

concepts.name: Vivid
concepts.definition: Vivid is the quality of energy stimulated within a particular modality, which relates to how much energy the computer is generating to stimulate that sensory organ.

concepts.name: Interactivity
concepts.definition: Interactivity refers to the capability of the user to make changes to the world, the response of virtual entities to user actions, and the user's ability to influence future events.

concepts.name: Presence
concepts.definition: Presence is a psychological state or subjective perception where the individual fails to accurately acknowledge the role of the technology in their current experience.

concepts.name: Qualities
concepts.definition: These qualities refer to the activation of one or more sensory organs in a suitable way.

concepts.name: Psychological side
concepts.definition: The psychological side is the domain of presence, relating to the user's subjective perception of the experience.

concepts.name: Overall goal of any virtual reality system
concepts.definition: The overall goal of any virtual reality system is to create a high degree of presence, making users feel they are in the virtual world and unable to distinguish it from the real world.

concepts.name: Representational fidelity
concepts.definition: Representational fidelity refers to the degree to which the VR experience conveys a place that is or could be on Earth, matching or exploiting the user's familiarity with that location.

concepts.name: Combine real and virtual worlds
concepts.definition: This requirement means that virtual content should be overlaid on the real world representation.

concepts.name: Interactive in real time
concepts.definition: This refers to supporting suitable forms of interaction so that the user can interact with the digital content overlaid on the real world representation.

concepts.name: Pose
concepts.definition: In this context, pose refers to two things: position and orientation.

concepts.name: Registration phase
concepts.definition: This phase determines the pose of a viewer with respect to the real world anchor.

concepts.name: Tracking phase
concepts.definition: This phase is necessary because the user is likely to move with an AR application, requiring continuous updates to the pose.

concepts.name: Immersion
concepts.definition: Immersion is tied to the technological aspect, the technological issues of VR.

concepts.name: Cyber sickness
concepts.definition: Cyber sickness is a concern that will be discussed in terms of its causes, measurement, and mitigation strategies.

concepts.name: Visually Induced Motion Sickness
concepts.definition: It is another name for cybersickness, a condition that can affect individuals when they interact with virtual reality technology.

concepts.name: Causes
concepts.definition: This refers to the factors that lead to cybersickness.

concepts.name: Evaluation
concepts.definition: This refers to how we measure or assess cybersickness.

concepts.name: Mitigation strategies
concepts.definition: These are strategies that can be adopted to overcome the challenges associated with cybersickness.

concepts.name: Stereoscopic vision
concepts.definition: Stereoscopic vision is the visual experience whose nature is determined by the distance between the eyes.

concepts.name: Latency
concepts.definition: Latency is the time delay between a user's movement in the physical world and the corresponding change in the virtual world.

concepts.name: Latency jitter
concepts.definition: Latency jitter is the variability in the time gap (latency) between a user's action in the physical world and its reflection in the virtual world.

concepts.name: Visual motion stimulus
concepts.definition: It is the movement experienced by the user in a virtual environment and is considered one of the primary causes of cyber sickness.

concepts.name: Vection
concepts.definition: Vection is the sensation of self-motion.

concepts.name: Sensory mismatch
concepts.definition: It occurs when users' virtual movements do not match their physical movements, resulting in discomfort and disorientation that leads to cyber sickness.

concepts.name: Teleportation
concepts.definition: Teleportation is an instantaneous transition between points in the virtual world.

concepts.name: Visual complexity
concepts.definition: It is a factor that is positively correlated to cyber sickness symptoms.

concepts.name: Physiological or biometric input
concepts.definition: These inputs are used to detect cybersickness and overcome the potential inaccuracies of subjective questionnaires.

concepts.name: Behavioral input
concepts.definition: Behavioral input is another category of data that can be used to measure cybersickness.

concepts.name: Content-based input
concepts.definition: Content-based input is a type of data that can be used to measure or evaluate cybersickness.

concepts.name: Postural sway
concepts.definition: This is a way to measure cybersickness by monitoring axial movements or changes in the user's center of pressure during VR exposure.

concepts.name: Optical flow
concepts.definition: This is the apparent motion perceived by VR users due to relative motion between the user and the environment.

concepts.name: Manual evaluation
concepts.definition: Manual evaluation is a measurement technique based on human intervention, typically involving the distribution and analysis of questionnaires.

concepts.name: Machine learning-based evaluation
concepts.definition: This evaluation method uses automated algorithms on the input data to measure cyber sickness.

concepts.name: Transparent models
concepts.definition: These models provide clear insight into the decision-making process and their inner workings can be easily understood.

concepts.name: cybersickness
concepts.definition: Cybersickness is the primary topic of discussion in this lecture segment.

concepts.name: evaluation techniques
concepts.definition: Evaluation techniques are methods used to measure and evaluate cybersickness.

concepts.name: input
concepts.definition: Input is one of the three broad aspects of evaluation, referring to the data provided.

concepts.name: process
concepts.definition: Process is one of the three broad aspects of evaluation, referring to the evaluation procedure itself.

concepts.name: output
concepts.definition: Output is one of the three broad aspects of evaluation, referring to the kind of results expected from the evaluation process.

concepts.name: Interpretable models
concepts.definition: These models offer more flexibility in customization and provide precise details about the relationships between the input and output.

concepts.name: Hybrid models
concepts.definition: They are combinations of different ML models designed to provide both high accuracy and transparency in their decision-making process.

concepts.name: Detection
concepts.definition: Detection refers to the process of identifying cyber sickness after it has already occurred.

concepts.name: Prediction
concepts.definition: Prediction involves anticipating cyber sickness before it happens.

concepts.name: Classification
concepts.definition: Classification indicates the likelihood or severity of CS.

concepts.name: Sickness score
concepts.definition: A sickness score quantifies the severity of the cyber sickness (CS) experience.

concepts.name: Severity of CS
concepts.definition: The severity of cyber sickness is assessed based on the scores or ratings provided.

concepts.name: Mitigation
concepts.definition: Mitigation is the third aspect of cyber sickness, focusing on measures taken to reduce or eliminate its impact when complete prevention is not possible.

concepts.name: Trade-off
concepts.definition: A trade-off is the decision of whether to completely avoid cyber sickness by reducing presence or to balance the compromise between the two.

concepts.name: Developer's perspective
concepts.definition: The developer's perspective focuses on what developers can do or how they can address the problem.

concepts.name: User's perspective
concepts.definition: The user's perspective focuses on what users can do, regardless of the quality of the solution.

concepts.name: FOV adjustment
concepts.definition: Adjusting the field of view means changing the amount of virtual environment visible at any moment, which can mitigate the onset or severity of cyber sickness.

concepts.name: Symmetric mask
concepts.definition: This is a technique where the periphery is occluded in reaction to translational and/or angular velocity.

concepts.name: Blurring
concepts.definition: Blurring means obscuring or reducing the clarity.

concepts.name: Depth of field blur
concepts.definition: Depth of field blur makes use of well-known depth cues in human vision.

concepts.name: Peripheral blur
concepts.definition: Peripheral blur is one of the two types of blur effects.

concepts.name: Rest frames
concepts.definition: Rest frames are fixed elements within the virtual environment that remain stationary relative to the real world regardless of the user's movements.

concepts.name: Independent visual backgrounds
concepts.definition: Independent visual backgrounds are rest frames attached to the head reference frame.

concepts.name: Simultaneous presentation of sound and vibration
concepts.definition: This involves providing sound and vibration at the same time.

concepts.name: Modified motion platforms
concepts.definition: These platforms can be modified to provide short bursts of rotational acceleration that match the visual forward acceleration.

concepts.name: Viewpoint snapping
concepts.definition: This technique involves rendering moving pictures in discrete chunks during rotation.

concepts.name: Habituation
concepts.definition: The intensity of cyber sickness gradually decreases after repeated experience in the virtual environment.

concepts.name: Slow diaphragmatic breathing
concepts.definition: Controlling breathing patterns to a large extent, reducing the possibility of cyber sickness.

concepts.name: External causes
concepts.definition: These causes can be related to hardware or content.

concepts.name: Evaluation strategies
concepts.definition: Evaluation strategies for measuring cybersickness involve defining the kind of input to the measurement process, the process itself (which can be manual or automated through machine learning approaches), and the resulting output (which can be classes, CS scores, or numerical values).

concepts.name: organism
concepts.definition: In the context of a VR system, the organism typically refers to the human user.

concepts.name: stimulation
concepts.definition: Stimulation is the process where the hardware produces stimuli that override the senses of the user.

concepts.name: Surrounding physical world
concepts.definition: The surrounding physical world is an element that should be taken into account as part of the overall VR system.

concepts.name: Head tracking
concepts.definition: Head tracking is the most important thing to track when discussing tracking in VR.

concepts.name: VR hardware
concepts.definition: VR hardware should not be restricted to only the computer, HMD, or controller used by the user.

concepts.name: Trackers
concepts.definition: Trackers or sensors are hardware components that can track objects in the surroundings rather than the user directly.

concepts.name: Display
concepts.definition: It can mean any device that produces output that stimulates users' sensory organs.

concepts.name: world grounded devices
concepts.definition: These are devices that are fixed in the real world and do not move.

concepts.name: non-tracked handheld controllers
concepts.definition: These are devices held in hand, but the system does not track their exact position in 3D space.

concepts.name: tracked handheld controllers
concepts.definition: These are devices that possess 6 degrees of freedom tracking, allowing their movements to be tracked by the system.

concepts.name: bend sensing gloves
concepts.definition: These gloves detect hand postures and gestures because sensors are placed at all bend positions or joints.

concepts.name: pinch gloves
concepts.definition: In pinch gloves, sensors are placed only at the fingertip positions, typically to detect pinching gestures.

concepts.name: bare hand inputs
concepts.definition: This method tracks the bare hand using computer vision techniques, allowing users to provide gestures without wearing external devices.

concepts.name: non-hand-based input devices
concepts.definition: These types of devices capture input from other parts of the body other than the hand.

concepts.name: head tracking based input devices
concepts.definition: These devices typically use our head motion for input.

concepts.name: eye trackers
concepts.definition: These devices are typically used to track eye movements, allowing the system to infer what to do and take necessary action.

concepts.name: Midas touch problem
concepts.definition: This is an issue where it is difficult to understand whether a user's action is intentional or by nature.

concepts.name: Full-body tracking
concepts.definition: This method tracks more than just the head and hands, which adds to the illusion of self-embodiment as well as social presence.

concepts.name: Motion capture suit
concepts.definition: A suit containing a network of straps with IMU sensors worn at different body parts that capture and transmit raw movement data converted to full body position and movement.

concepts.name: Camera-based tracking
concepts.definition: This approach uses multiple surrounding cameras to detect the movement of fiducial markers worn by an actor to infer the overall body movement of the character.

concepts.name: Voice or speech or sound tracking
concepts.definition: This input type captures voice, speech, and non-speech sound as input for interaction in the virtual world.

concepts.name: Computer
concepts.definition: A device that processes data coming from input sensors and then activates or actuates the output devices.

concepts.name: GPU
concepts.definition: A graphics processing unit typically used to speed up the rendering process due to its inherent parallel processing abilities.

concepts.name: Multicore processor
concepts.definition: A processor that can greatly increase computational capacity and support tasks better than non-multicore or unicore processors.

concepts.name: Head-mounted displays
concepts.definition: HMDs are wearable and mobile displays meant to stimulate the visual sense.

concepts.name: World-fixed displays
concepts.definition: World-fixed displays are stationary displays that are not wearable and render graphics onto surfaces that do not move with the head.

concepts.name: Monoscopic viewing
concepts.definition: Monoscopic viewing is the process of viewing images when the display is using only one screen.

concepts.name: Stereoscopic viewing
concepts.definition: Stereoscopic viewing is the process of viewing images when the display is using two screens.

concepts.name: Haptics
concepts.definition: Haptics are outputs that explore our touch perception.

concepts.name: Passive device
concepts.definition: Passive devices are static physical objects.

concepts.name: Active device
concepts.definition: Active devices are physical feedback controlled by the computer.

concepts.name: Tactile
concepts.definition: Tactile refers to touch sensations obtained through the skin.

concepts.name: Self-grounded device
concepts.definition: Self-grounded devices are worn or held by and move with the user.

concepts.name: Passive motion platform
concepts.definition: A motion platform that is controlled by the user, without direct computer control.

concepts.name: Omnidirectional treadmills
concepts.definition: A type of treadmill that is quite common in virtual reality systems.

concepts.name: Proprioceptive forces
concepts.definition: One of the types of output devices used in VR systems.

concepts.name: Headsets and glasses
concepts.definition: This is a category of augmented reality devices used to provide AR experience.

concepts.name: Handheld devices
concepts.definition: This is a category of augmented reality devices, such as smartphones and tablets.

concepts.name: Projection-based systems
concepts.definition: This is a category of augmented reality devices that includes projection keyboards, interactive projectors, AR sandboxes, industrial AR systems, and medical systems.

concepts.name: Spatial AR
concepts.definition: Spatial AR devices include interactive projectors.

concepts.name: Head-up displays
concepts.definition: Head-up displays are devices typically found in cars.

concepts.name: AR contact lenses
concepts.definition: This is the latest technology being explored for AR systems, with ongoing research by various companies.

concepts.name: Projection keyboard
concepts.definition: This is a system that projects a virtual keyboard onto any surface, allowing users to type as if they were using a physical keyboard.

concepts.name: Interactive projector
concepts.definition: It projects images onto any surface, thereby turning that surface into an interactive display and creating an AR experience.

concepts.name: AR headsets
concepts.definition: AR headsets are generally larger and more immersive, combining both real-world content and augmented digital content.

concepts.name: glasses
concepts.definition: These are special types of glasses where real digital content can be projected on top of our regular real-world view.

concepts.name: high-definition holograms
concepts.definition: High-definition holograms or digital content are integrated with the real-world view.

concepts.name: interaction
concepts.definition: The interaction in the case of HoloLens takes place through detection of eye movements, voice commands, and hand gestures.

concepts.name: smart glasses
concepts.definition: Smart glasses are typically lighter than AR HMDs, resemble standard eyeglasses, and provide simpler heads-up display type AR digital content overlays.

concepts.name: Augmentation
concepts.definition: The process where digital content is overlaid onto the live streaming of the real world environment.

concepts.name: Marker-based AR
concepts.definition: A type of AR where the system recognizes specific markers placed in the real world to augment content.

concepts.name: Spatial augmented reality devices
concepts.definition: The third category of AR devices mentioned in the lecture.

concepts.name: Computer vision techniques
concepts.definition: These are advanced techniques typically used in spatial AR systems to achieve seamless mixing.

concepts.name: Room-scale AR or tabletop AR
concepts.definition: These are alternative names for the devices being discussed in this segment.

concepts.name: Seamless mixing
concepts.definition: Seamless mixing is the successful integration of virtual and physical elements, which is possible when the necessary conditions are met.

concepts.name: Depth sensors
concepts.definition: These are advanced sensors typically used in spatial AR systems to achieve seamless mixing.

concepts.name: Multi-user engagement with AR systems
concepts.definition: This is the characteristic where multiple users can work together on the augmented digital content.

concepts.name: Spatial AR systems
concepts.definition: Spatial AR systems are characterized by distinct features and functionalities.

concepts.name: HUDs
concepts.definition: HUDs are commonly seen in cars and are also frequently used in aircraft.

concepts.name: Sensing
concepts.definition: Sensing is another term often used to describe the requirement of tracking in XR systems.

concepts.name: Tracking hardware
concepts.definition: Tracking hardware refers to the entire hardware components typically used in XR applications for tracking.

concepts.name: User's pose, position, and orientation
concepts.definition: These are the specific elements that AR requires keeping track of.

concepts.name: Tracking of the user's sense organs
concepts.definition: This category involves tracking the user's sense organs.

concepts.name: Tracking the user's other body parts
concepts.definition: This category tracks body parts other than sense organs, which is required when the user wants to see a representation of the body in the virtual world.

concepts.name: Tracking the rest of the environment
concepts.definition: This category involves tracking the surrounding environment that is not related to the user.

concepts.name: Outside-in tracking
concepts.definition: This type of tracking occurs when the trackers or sensors are placed within the real world external to the user, not attached to the user.

concepts.name: Calibration
concepts.definition: Calibration is the process of transforming sensor output to behave as closely to the real value as possible.

concepts.name: Registration
concepts.definition: Registration is the step where the initial sensor position and orientation are estimated or determined.

concepts.name: Integration
concepts.definition: Integration is the step where sensory measurements are aggregated or combined at discrete points of time.

concepts.name: Drift correction
concepts.definition: Drift correction means compensating for differences between the estimated tracking and the actual position and orientation.

concepts.name: Inside-out tracking
concepts.definition: In inside-out tracking, the tracker carries the sensors that are part of the devices that the user is wearing or using.

concepts.name: Inside-out
concepts.definition: Inside-out trackers have all the sensors placed on the device that the user is using.

concepts.name: Outside-in
concepts.definition: Outside-in trackers have sensors placed in the surrounding environment rather than on the device that the user is using.

concepts.name: IMU sensor
concepts.definition: An IMU sensor is a composite hardware containing three types of sensors: gyroscope, accelerometer, and magnetometer.

concepts.name: gyroscope
concepts.definition: A gyroscope is a sensor that captures the angular velocity.

concepts.name: accelerometer
concepts.definition: An accelerometer is a sensor that captures the linear acceleration along the three axes (x, y, and z).

concepts.name: magnetometer
concepts.definition: A magnetometer is a sensor that captures magnetic field strength along the three axes.

concepts.name: Measurement error
concepts.definition: Measurement error is the difference between the measured angular velocity ($\omega_g$) and the actual angular velocity ($\omega_a$).

concepts.name: Linear relationship
concepts.definition: A linear relationship is a proposed mathematical model between the measured angular velocity ($\omega_g$) and the actual angular velocity ($\omega_a$) in the form $\omega_g = a + b \cdot \omega_a$.

concepts.name: Linear least squares
concepts.definition: Linear least squares is a classical regression problem used to optimize the square term of the difference between the sensor readings during calibration.

concepts.name: Initial orientation
concepts.definition: The initial orientation is the direction the headset is facing when the tracking system is turned on, which sets the initial alignment.

concepts.name: Alignment
concepts.definition: Alignment is the setting of the initial alignment between the real and virtual worlds, represented symbolically by theta at time t=0.

concepts.name: Calibrated angular velocity sample
concepts.definition: This is the angular velocity sample obtained from the gyroscopic sensor at a specific instant.

concepts.name: gain parameter
concepts.definition: The gain parameter (alpha) is a normalized value between 0 to 1 used to combine individually computed orientations.

concepts.name: theta dk
concepts.definition: Theta dk is the drift-corrected orientation at time instant t.

concepts.name: theta gk
concepts.definition: Theta gk is the orientation obtained by integrating gyroscope values at the kth instant.

concepts.name: theta ck
concepts.definition: Theta ck is the orientation obtained with camera at kth instant.

concepts.name: Electromechanical trackers
concepts.definition: These trackers consist of a serial or parallel kinematic structure composed of links that are interconnected using joints with sensors.

concepts.name: World-fixed
concepts.definition: This type of electromechanical tracker is a setup that is not worn on the body of the user.

concepts.name: Wearable trackers
concepts.definition: These are electromechanical trackers that can be worn on the body of the user.

concepts.name: Electromagnetic trackers
concepts.definition: It is a kind of non-contact position measurement device that uses a magnetic field from a stationary transmitter to determine the real-time position of a moving receiver element.

concepts.name: Acoustic tracking
concepts.definition: This tracking method uses ultrasonic signals produced by stationary transmitters to determine the real-time position.

concepts.name: Ultrasonic tracking
concepts.definition: This is a method that uses ultrasonic signals produced by stationary transmitters to determine real time position.

concepts.name: Non-contact position measurement device
concepts.definition: This device tracks position without physical contact, such as electromagnetic trackers.

concepts.name: vision-based tracker
concepts.definition: A vision-based tracker is a category of tracking system that is probably the most important in the present context.

concepts.name: optical sensors
concepts.definition: These sensors are deployed to detect or track the pose.

concepts.name: infrared tracking
concepts.definition: This is a vision-based tracking technique that uses targets that emit or reflect light.

concepts.name: outside looking in
concepts.definition: In this method, targets are attached to objects being tracked, but the cameras are external to the object and placed in the environment.

concepts.name: Fiducials
concepts.definition: Fiducials are artificial landmarks added to the environment to aid in registration and tracking.

concepts.name: Fiducial tracking
concepts.definition: Fiducial tracking involves adding artificial landmarks in the environment so that one can track whatever is desired.

concepts.name: SLAM
concepts.definition: SLAM (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping) is a technique that simultaneously creates and updates a map of the real environment while localizing positions within it.

concepts.name: 3D structure tracking
concepts.definition: This technique involves creating 3D models of the structures present in the environment and using them for augmentation of the real-world view.

concepts.name: 3D models
concepts.definition: These are high-quality representations created from data obtained by sensors of real objects and environments.

concepts.name: Augmentation of the real-world view
concepts.definition: This is the process of using 3D models of environmental structures to enhance the real-world view.

concepts.name: inertial trackers
concepts.definition: These are self-contained sensors that measure rate of change in object orientation, translation velocity, or acceleration.

concepts.name: primary sensors
concepts.definition: These are the basic sensors used in inertial tracking, specifically gyroscopes, accelerometer, and magnetometer.

concepts.name: acoustic sensing
concepts.definition: This is one type of sensing that does not directly fit into the previously listed categories of trackers.

concepts.name: GPS
concepts.definition: GPS is a positional tracking device that allows us to track positions.

concepts.name: RTK
concepts.definition: RTK, or real time kinematic technology, uses GPS signal carrier waves for measurement to provide further accuracy compared to the basic GPS system.

concepts.name: Motion capture
concepts.definition: The technique of digitally recording movements of real things, usually humans.

concepts.name: Eye-tracking systems
concepts.definition: Trackers that typically track the gaze point or area of the gaze of the user.

concepts.name: Non-real-time tracking
concepts.definition: Tracking that does not need to be real-time.

concepts.name: Hybrid trackers
concepts.definition: Any other tracker that can be roughly called hybrid.

concepts.name: VR software
concepts.definition: The role of VR software is to drive the hardware to generate an experience utilizing our senses.

concepts.name: Modeling of the environment
concepts.definition: Modeling of the environment is the activity of creating the virtual environment.

concepts.name: Rendering
concepts.definition: Rendering is the creation of the stereoscopic view, which refers broadly to output for various senses.

concepts.name: Perceptual design
concepts.definition: Perceptual design ensures that stimuli generated by the hardware can suitably stimulate our sense organs.

concepts.name: VR engine
concepts.definition: The VR engine is one of the two components that make up the software part of the system.

concepts.name: High-level descriptions
concepts.definition: Descriptions provided by the developer that the supporting software automatically converts into low-level details.

concepts.name: Middleware
concepts.definition: A layer that can exist between the developer and the hardware.

concepts.name: Software development kit
concepts.definition: A kit utilized for particular headsets that handles low-level operations such as device drivers, head tracking, and display output.

concepts.name: Platform
concepts.definition: A combination of hardware and OS upon which SDKs are dependent.

concepts.name: Game engine
concepts.definition: Middleware specifically created or adapted for VR experience generation.

concepts.name: Virtual World Generator
concepts.definition: The VWG is an abstraction of the whole software system whose key role is to maintain internal reality and convert input information to output so that it appears real to the user.

concepts.name: Internal reality
concepts.definition: Internal reality is the state that the VWG must maintain so that the virtual world appears real to the user.

concepts.name: Abstraction
concepts.definition: The whole software system can be thought of as an abstraction, specifically a virtual world generation abstraction.

concepts.name: Input/output match
concepts.definition: The role of the VR VWG is to maintain the match between the input information and the resulting output.

concepts.name: Input events
concepts.definition: Input events are data arriving from low-level systems that must be arranged in a queue ready to be processed systematically.

concepts.name: Queue
concepts.definition: A queue is a mechanism used to arrange multiple simultaneous input events so that they can be processed systematically.

concepts.name: Haptic renderer
concepts.definition: A device that generates haptic display to be sensed with our skin.

concepts.name: Triangular mesh
concepts.definition: A structure of numerous triangles in a 3D space that must be created to form a synthetic scene.

concepts.name: Computer graphics
concepts.definition: The field that addresses computer-generated images from synthetic models.

concepts.name: Texture mapping
concepts.definition: The process of taking camera images of a real object and mapping them onto a synthetic object in the virtual world.

concepts.name: matched motion
concepts.definition: It is the correspondence maintained between user motions in the real and virtual world.

concepts.name: matched zone
concepts.definition: It is a region where the real and virtual worlds perfectly align, and the user's physical movement is restricted.

concepts.name: locomotion
concepts.definition: It is moving oneself in the virtual world while the motion is not matched in the real world.

concepts.name: User locomotion
concepts.definition: User locomotion is the method of moving oneself within the virtual world, often by operating input devices like controllers or keyboards.

concepts.name: Avatar
concepts.definition: The avatar is the user's representation in the virtual world that can perform activities like walking, running, or swimming without the user moving physically.

concepts.name: Vehicle metaphor
concepts.definition: The vehicle metaphor is a way to allow the user to move in the virtual world by operating the controls of a virtual vehicle while remaining seated.

concepts.name: Key components
concepts.definition: Key components are the essential elements that VR software should support, primarily from the developer's point of view.

concepts.name: Desirable components of the virtual world generator
concepts.definition: Components that are considered beneficial or ideal additions to the virtual world generator abstraction.

concepts.name: Synthetic virtual world generation
concepts.definition: The generation of a virtual world that requires support for computer graphics operations.

concepts.name: Matched motion and locomotion
concepts.definition: Matched motion and locomotion refers to specific concepts for which support is required within the virtual world generator abstraction.

concepts.name: Physics support
concepts.definition: Physics support is a required functionality whose basic idea is to make the virtual world appear to behave like the real world.

concepts.name: Collision
concepts.definition: Collision is the event of one object interacting with other objects.

concepts.name: Collision detection algorithm
concepts.definition: The collision detection algorithm determines whether two or more bodies are intersecting in the virtual world and how they should behave if they are.

concepts.name: Collision response
concepts.definition: Collision response is the appropriate action that must occur after a collision takes place.

concepts.name: Shared virtual world
concepts.definition: A virtual world that is maintained by a system or a server.

concepts.name: Matched zone
concepts.definition: A matched zone is a distinct area assigned to each user that exists in the real world, which may overlap or be disjoint and distributed around the earth.

concepts.name: Collaborative VR experience
concepts.definition: A collaborative experience that is created over a network.

concepts.name: Physics
concepts.definition: The algorithms and support required to handle problems such as avatar movement, collision detection, and the response to collisions.

concepts.name: Game engine
concepts.definition: A popular engine adapted to work for virtual reality that comes with built-in supports for features like collisions and physics.

concepts.name: Native application
concepts.definition: A native application requires the use of SDKs that are tailored specifically to the platform and the hardware.

concepts.name: HMD
concepts.definition: HMDs, or head-mounted displays, are the most popular device types used for VR experiences.

concepts.name: Cloud hosting and rendering
concepts.definition: These tools only provide support for hosting and rendering over a network.

concepts.name: Libraries
concepts.definition: Libraries are tools used for development support, specifically for deployment over the web.

concepts.name: SDKs
concepts.definition: SDKs are one of two developer choices for building VR applications, allowing development from scratch.

concepts.name: Deployment tools
concepts.definition: These are tools available for deploying applications, either on native systems or over the web.

concepts.name: low-level software libraries
concepts.definition: These libraries require considerable skill from the developer, both in understanding the library functions and in coding to call them.

concepts.name: simple authoring tools
concepts.definition: These tools assume that the developer does not have any programming skill and are typically intended for novice developers or users.

concepts.name: Framework for AR system development
concepts.definition: This is a combination of multiple libraries created to overcome the limitations of standard toolkits and enable realistic AR system development.

concepts.name: Scene graphs
concepts.definition: Scene graphs represent computer graphic scenes as a node-based graph, allowing the entire scene to be represented as a tree with nodes and links.

concepts.name: 3D registration
concepts.definition: 3D registration is the process of creating and rendering a 3D object at a specific position based on tracking data.

concepts.name: Low-level OpenGL-based rendering support
concepts.definition: Low-level OpenGL-based rendering support is the type of rendering support provided by the toolkit.

concepts.name: ARToolKit
concepts.definition: This library is primarily meant to provide tracking support for developing AR applications.

concepts.name: Rapid prototyping
concepts.definition: The process of rapidly visualizing or creating prototypes of an idea before undertaking major coding development, which helps determine if the idea is viable.

concepts.name: FLAR Toolkit
concepts.definition: A version of an AR toolkit ported over to Flash that allows users to have an AR experience from within their web browser.

concepts.name: Flash AR Manager
concepts.definition: A framework that combines a variety of different AR tracking and graphics libraries together, primarily for prototyping purposes.

concepts.name: Open Frameworks
concepts.definition: It is an open-source C++ middleware library that is a combination of multiple libraries meant for desktop and mobile platforms.

concepts.name: Client device
concepts.definition: A mobile device that is primarily treated as a client device, meaning actual computation may take place on a backend server.

concepts.name: Rendering device
concepts.definition: A mobile device that is primarily treated as a rendering device, handling visual output.

concepts.name: Backend server
concepts.definition: A server where actual computation may take place, rather than on the mobile device.

concepts.name: Plugins to existing tools
concepts.definition: Plugins are additions that provide AR-specific functionalities to software tools that the user is already familiar with.

concepts.name: AR visualization
concepts.definition: AR visualization is a capability supported by AR-based plugins within interactive 3D graphics authoring tools.

concepts.name: Plugin-based approach
concepts.definition: This approach provides an easy and quick method for developing AR applications, but it can limit flexibility in design and depend on proprietary software.

concepts.name: Authoring tool
concepts.definition: An authoring tool is a graphics tool used to create interactive 3D applications and provides underlying support for development.

concepts.name: Proprietary player software
concepts.definition: This is software that content produced with an authoring tool must depend on in most cases to be played.

concepts.name: Low-level software development tools
concepts.definition: These tools allow developers to build their own system from scratch rather than depending on a third-party tool to resolve issues with high-level tools.

concepts.name: Plugins
concepts.definition: Plugins require a basic authoring tool to function, providing AR support through that underlying tool.

concepts.name: Graphical user interface
concepts.definition: These are typically drag-and-drop type interfaces that allow developers to create an experience without requiring coding.

concepts.name: Web-based authoring tool
concepts.definition: This is an authoring tool that operates via the web, such as Wikitude Studio.

concepts.name: Categories
concepts.definition: These are classifications of tools and packages based on the programming skill required to use them.

concepts.name: Low-level libraries and frameworks
concepts.definition: These are tools that require the highest programming skill to deal with.

concepts.name: Rapid prototyping tools
concepts.definition: These are tools that fall into a category between the extremes of high and low programming skill requirements.

concepts.name: Human factors
concepts.definition: Human factors are elements that affect the user's experience within Extended Reality systems, such as virtual reality or augmented reality.

concepts.name: Technology disappearing
concepts.definition: The vision of making the technology disappear from the user's point of view.

concepts.name: IoT or ubiquitous computing
concepts.definition: A state where each user can have access to multiple connected computers that communicate with each other so the user does not have to separately operate them.

concepts.name: Interactive computing systems
concepts.definition: Systems where interaction takes place between the computer or the system and the user.

concepts.name: Lay person
concepts.definition: A user who is not necessarily an expert in the technology but simply wants to use the system.

concepts.name: Interactions
concepts.definition: Interactions are designed to fulfill the needs of the users by taking them to the desired system states.

concepts.name: Interactive system
concepts.definition: When designing interactive systems intended for laypersons, the system should not require the user to learn about the underlying technology or understand relevant technical terms.

concepts.name: Layouts
concepts.definition: Layouts are the way the elements are organized on the screen or on the interface that meet the user's expectations.

concepts.name: System state
concepts.definition: The system state is what exactly is happening from the point of view of the user, not from the point of view of technical details.

concepts.name: Goal state
concepts.definition: The goal state is the state reached after transitioning from one state to another until the user reaches some goal.

concepts.name: Interface elements
concepts.definition: Interface elements are the elements with which the user interacts that are acceptable to the users.

concepts.name: user characteristics
concepts.definition: This is the knowledge of the user that must be utilized to build the system.

concepts.name: human-computer interaction
concepts.definition: It is a discipline concerned with the design, evaluation, and implementation of interactive computing systems for human use and with the study of major phenomena surrounding them.

concepts.name: core concern
concepts.definition: The core concern is incorporating humans into the design.

concepts.name: human factors
concepts.definition: Human factors is presented as an important issue in the context of the lecture.

concepts.name: Novice
concepts.definition: Novice users are those who are using the system for the first time.

concepts.name: Intermittent
concepts.definition: Intermittent users are those who use the system occasionally.

concepts.name: Expert
concepts.definition: Expert users are individuals who are experts in using the system, rather than technology experts, having used the system regularly over a long period of time.

concepts.name: Usability
concepts.definition: It is the extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals, with effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction in a specified context of use.

concepts.name: User interface or user experience designer
concepts.definition: Such a designer is primarily concerned about the design of the interface elements and layouts, which is mostly a creative design aspect, informed by user characteristics.

concepts.name: Industrial product designer
concepts.definition: This designer refers to the form of the product that is shape, size and look.

concepts.name: Electronic engineer
concepts.definition: This designer might look at it as adding more features at the hardware level such as more sensors, smaller chips to reduce size and more power efficient battery, primarily from the hardware point of view.

concepts.name: Development lifecycle
concepts.definition: This is a process that takes care of the user characteristics to better match the user's needs and expectations.

concepts.name: Effectiveness
concepts.definition: Effectiveness refers to whether the user is able to do whatever they want to do.

concepts.name: Efficiency
concepts.definition: Efficiency refers to how fast the user can do what they want to do.

concepts.name: Satisfaction
concepts.definition: Satisfaction refers to how satisfied the user is when they are using the system.

concepts.name: User-centered design
concepts.definition: User-centered design indicates the involvement of users, either in an active or passive manner, in the design lifecycle itself.

concepts.name: Extended reality systems
concepts.definition: The core concern of extended reality software is to create a relationship between the user and the virtual environment.

concepts.name: Interaction design and modeling
concepts.definition: This approach assists the user to provide input data seamlessly, effectively, and easily from the user's point of view.

concepts.name: Perceptual design and modeling
concepts.definition: Perceptual design and modeling is crucial because it addresses how well the output is generated, focusing on generating appropriate stimuli and ensuring they are appropriately perceived.

concepts.name: XR engine
concepts.definition: The XR engine, which is the middleware, utilizes the hardware resources to generate output.

concepts.name: interactive systems
concepts.definition: Interactive systems are a topic that includes their basic idea, how they differ from other systems, their design concerns, why they are important, and how XR relates to their development.

concepts.name: Human factors
concepts.definition: Human factors are the considerations relevant to Extended Reality (XR) that inform developers on how to build better XR systems.

concepts.name: Interaction design
concepts.definition: Interaction design is important to give the user the ease of interacting with the system.

concepts.name: Illusion of reality
concepts.definition: The interaction and perceptual stimuli are supposed to be designed to create the best possible illusion of reality.

concepts.name: Immersion
concepts.definition: The feeling of perceiving that we are immersed.

concepts.name: Perceptual system
concepts.definition: The system that works by how our senses function and the physiology that drives our perception.

concepts.name: Virtual world
concepts.definition: The artificial world that our bodies are not designed to perceive.

concepts.name: perceptual psychology
concepts.definition: It is the science of understanding how the brain converts sensory stimulation into perceived phenomena.

concepts.name: Sensor
concepts.definition: When referring to a device or system, a sensor is a device that converts an energy source into electrical signals in a circuit.

concepts.name: Human bodily sensors
concepts.definition: In the context of the human body, these refer to an organ that converts a stimulus into neural impulses.

concepts.name: Photoreceptors
concepts.definition: Photoreceptors are the receptors that are part of the sense, and the eye is the sense organ.

concepts.name: Mechanoreceptors
concepts.definition: Mechanoreceptors are receptors that respond to physical stimuli such as air pressure waves (auditory), tissue distortion (touch), or gravity/acceleration (balance).

concepts.name: Thermoreceptors
concepts.definition: These are one of the two types of receptors involved in the touch sense.

concepts.name: Chemoreceptors
concepts.definition: These are receptors used in the sense of taste and smell, where chemical composition serves as the stimulus.

concepts.name: Sensory system selectivity
concepts.definition: This is the phenomenon where a receptor is designed to be activated only when a specific type of stimulus arrives.

concepts.name: Receptors
concepts.definition: Receptors are bodily organs or sensors designed to be activated only when a specific type of stimulus arrives.

concepts.name: Perception
concepts.definition: Perception is a higher level activity that occurs after sense organs convert stimuli into neural impulses.

concepts.name: Cerebral cortex
concepts.definition: The cerebral cortex is the part of the brain that handles perception and other functions like attention, memory, language, and consciousness.

concepts.name: Dendrites
concepts.definition: Dendrites are the input edges to the node (cell body).

concepts.name: Axon
concepts.definition: Axons are the output edges of the neuron.

concepts.name: Synapse
concepts.definition: The synapse is the gap between the axon of one neuron and the dendrite of the next neuron through which electrical or chemical signals are passed.

concepts.name: Sensory organs
concepts.definition: These are the organs whose workings and implications for system design will be covered in detail in subsequent lectures.

concepts.name: Hierarchical processing
concepts.definition: This type of processing works in stages, allowing increasingly complex patterns to be detected in the stimulus.

concepts.name: Selectivity
concepts.definition: Selectivity is the idea that each receptor is susceptible to only one kind of stimulus.

concepts.name: Lower-level information
concepts.definition: This is the information derived directly from the initial inputs of receptors, such as R1 and R2.

concepts.name: Stimuli interpretation
concepts.definition: Stimuli interpretation is not based only on sensory inputs, but also depends on the kind of real-life experience knowledge a person possesses.

concepts.name: Perceptual phenomena
concepts.definition: Perceptual phenomena are the results of the combination of sensory input and knowledge, such as face recognition or identification of a song.

concepts.name: Perceptual processing
concepts.definition: Perceptual processing is the outcome of hierarchical processing combined with real-time sensory input and long-term knowledge or experience.

concepts.name: Long-term memory
concepts.definition: Long-term memory is knowledge or experience that has been gained or learned over a long period of time.

concepts.name: sixth sense
concepts.definition: It is a sense where we do not have a dedicated sensory organ or dedicated receptors to receive the stimuli, but we process information sent by the motor cortex.

concepts.name: Brain development
concepts.definition: It is basically learning the process of perception and learning the process of cognition over a long period of time.

concepts.name: Human physiology
concepts.definition: It is one of the basic components learned in the lecture, alongside psychology, in the context of designing VR systems.

concepts.name: Natural lenses
concepts.definition: Natural lenses are parts of the eyes.

concepts.name: Combined system
concepts.definition: The combined system of engineered and natural lenses helps us perceive the immersive visual content.

concepts.name: Visual perception
concepts.definition: Visual perception is the result when light is guided by lenses and arrives on the retina.

concepts.name: Retina
concepts.definition: This is the component at the back side of the eye where images are focused.

concepts.name: photons
concepts.definition: Photons are tiny particles of energy moving through space at high speeds.

concepts.name: waves
concepts.definition: Waves are ripples through space.

concepts.name: rays
concepts.definition: A ray is a path which is assumed to be created by a single hypothetical photon.

concepts.name: transmission
concepts.definition: Transmission is when light passes through the material and goes out of the material.

concepts.name: absorption
concepts.definition: Absorption is when the light rays terminate within the material or object.

concepts.name: reflection
concepts.definition: Reflection occurs when the ray falls on the surface and gets reflected from the surface without entering or penetrating the object.

concepts.name: Ambient light
concepts.definition: Ambient light is the light in the environment which gets reflected from the object surface along with light coming from the direct source.

concepts.name: Perceived color
concepts.definition: The perceived color is determined by the intensity of the light that reaches the viewer's eye.

concepts.name: Intensity of light that reaches the viewer's eye
concepts.definition: The intensity of the light that reaches the eye determines what color we are going to perceive.

concepts.name: Human vision system
concepts.definition: This is the system that the lecture will delve deeper into to gain a better understanding.

concepts.name: Vision physiology
concepts.definition: This is the specific aspect of vision that needs to be understood.

concepts.name: Refraction
concepts.definition: This is the process by which light rays are bent by the cornea and lens to focus images on the retina.

concepts.name: Pupil
concepts.definition: The pupil size can be changed (dilated or constricted) to let in more or less light.

concepts.name: Iris
concepts.definition: The iris controls the amount of light entering the eye by dilating or constricting the pupil size.

concepts.name: Rods
concepts.definition: Rods are photoreceptors that are more numerous in the peripheral region of the retina.

concepts.name: Cones
concepts.definition: Cones are photoreceptors mainly located in a small central region of the retina called the fovea.

concepts.name: Fovea
concepts.definition: The central region of the retina that has the greatest concentration of cones.

concepts.name: Photopic vision
concepts.definition: Photopic vision is the type of vision accomplished only with cones.

concepts.name: Scotopic vision
concepts.definition: Scotopic vision is the type of vision accomplished with rods only.

concepts.name: Aqueous humor
concepts.definition: Aqueous humor is a semi-liquid material found between the cornea and pupil.

concepts.name: Vitreous humor
concepts.definition: Vitreous humor is the material found between the lens and retina.

concepts.name: Image acuity
concepts.definition: Image acuity is aided by the structure where one optic nerve is dedicated to each cone.

concepts.name: visible light
concepts.definition: Visible light refers to a spectrum or range of frequencies of electromagnetic light waves that we are able to perceive.

concepts.name: perception of color
concepts.definition: The perception of color is the process where light waves excite the cones in our eye.

concepts.name: Central vision
concepts.definition: Vision supported by the concentration of cones in the fovea, requiring the eyes to be pointed straight at a target to perceive a sharp color image.

concepts.name: Peripheral vision
concepts.definition: Vision supported by the peripheral region of the retina, which is better at detecting movement but cannot distinguish colors effectively.

concepts.name: Peripheral region
concepts.definition: The area of the retina where photoreceptor density is less, containing a mix of rods and an even lesser amount of cones.

concepts.name: blind spot
concepts.definition: The blind spot is a region in the eye where there are no photoreceptors, meaning we are blind to the light or visual stimuli that fall in that area.

concepts.name: Human lens
concepts.definition: It is a natural lens with variable focal depth.

concepts.name: Image surface
concepts.definition: It is the portion of the eye where the light rays fall, which is a non-planar surface.

concepts.name: Engineered lens
concepts.definition: An artificially created lens used in the setup.

concepts.name: Focal depth
concepts.definition: The distance between the lens and the focal point.

concepts.name: Refractive index
concepts.definition: The amount of light that passes through a medium.

concepts.name: Focal plane
concepts.definition: The plane where the converging parallel lights meet.

concepts.name: Cornea
concepts.definition: The cornea is considered one of the two effective convex lenses in the eye.

concepts.name: Focal point
concepts.definition: The focal point is the retina center onto which light is converged.

concepts.name: Convergence
concepts.definition: Convergence is the process required to cause parallel rays of light to be focused onto the retina center.

concepts.name: Combined power
concepts.definition: Combined power is the total optical power achieved when the diopters of the cornea and natural lens are added together.

concepts.name: VR headset
concepts.definition: A VR headset is an engineered setup that places a screen close to the eyes, where the screen renders the image and a convex lens focuses the light onto the retina.

concepts.name: Convex lens
concepts.definition: A lens used to increase optical power, functioning similarly to reading glasses, and helping focus the image onto the retina.

concepts.name: Virtual image
concepts.definition: The image that the screen appears to project, which is perceived as being enormous and infinitely far away.

concepts.name: Artificial system
concepts.definition: The setup comprising the screen and the engineered lens whose objective is to convert light into normal light that falls on the eye for perception.

concepts.name: Binocular vision
concepts.definition: This is the state where both eyes are used to see the same image within a common region.

concepts.name: Translational
concepts.definition: Translational movement is used for navigating in the 3D space.

concepts.name: Rotational
concepts.definition: Rotational movement is primarily used for moving at different angles along the translational axis.

concepts.name: Degrees of freedom
concepts.definition: Degrees of freedom is an indication of the different ways an object can move in space.

concepts.name: Yaw
concepts.definition: Yaw is one of the three rotational degrees of freedom.

concepts.name: Roll
concepts.definition: Roll is one of the three rotational degrees of freedom.

concepts.name: Pitch
concepts.definition: Pitch is one of the three rotational degrees of freedom.

concepts.name: Photoreceptor density
concepts.definition: A basic physiological property that directly impacts the engineering requirements for visual display hardware.

concepts.name: Spatial resolution
concepts.definition: The consideration of how many pixels per square area are needed.

concepts.name: Intensity resolution and range
concepts.definition: The measure of how many intensity values can be produced and what the minimum and maximum intensity values are.

concepts.name: Temporal resolution
concepts.definition: The consideration of how fast displays need to change their pixels.

concepts.name: Frame rates
concepts.definition: The rate at which displays refresh their pixels, which is particularly important in the context of motion perception.

concepts.name: Aliasing
concepts.definition: Aliasing is the appearance of jagged lines or staircases instead of smooth lines, especially when zooming out.

concepts.name: Screen door effect
concepts.definition: The screen door effect is an important visual effect that appears as if there is a screen on top of the image.

concepts.name: Retina display
concepts.definition: A retina display is a type of display where the supported resolution is a minimum of 326 pixels per linear inch (ppi).

concepts.name: Auditory senses
concepts.definition: The topic of the lecture, which involves discussing the auditory sense and physiology of hearing and its relevance for extended reality experiences.

concepts.name: Human factors
concepts.definition: The ideas that influence the design and overall experience of interactive systems.

concepts.name: Extended reality systems
concepts.definition: Extended reality systems are environments or systems for which human factors, such as auditory senses, are relevant to the overall experience.

concepts.name: Audio recording and reproduction
concepts.definition: The process of recording sound (speech or non-speech) and reproducing it, which can be considered a VR experience in itself.

concepts.name: Believable experience
concepts.definition: An experience that is reinforced by audio, making it closer to reality and closer to everyday experiences.

concepts.name: Emotional connection
concepts.definition: An attachment to the environment that can be increased when vision is coupled with audio.

concepts.name: Sound
concepts.definition: Sound is nothing but vibration in a medium, which can be air, water, or other gases, liquids, and solids.

concepts.name: Sound wave
concepts.definition: A sound wave is a plot of pressure variation against time.

concepts.name: Frequency
concepts.definition: Frequency is the number of alterations between one maximum to another maximum per second, measured in Hertz.

concepts.name: Amplitude
concepts.definition: Amplitude is defined as the maximum displacement from the mean or rest position of the wave.

concepts.name: Phase
concepts.definition: Phase is the start position of a cycle of the wave, which can begin at 0 to 360 degrees.

concepts.name: Decompression extreme
concepts.definition: Decompression extreme, also called rarefaction extreme, means the pressure is very low.

concepts.name: canal
concepts.definition: The canal works as an amplifier, boosting the sound pressure for a range of frequencies.

concepts.name: tympanic membrane
concepts.definition: The tympanic membrane is the membrane that vibrates when struck by the wave.

concepts.name: ossicles
concepts.definition: Ossicles are three bones—malleus, incus, and stapes—that are part of the middle ear and are housed in an air-filled chamber.

concepts.name: cochlea
concepts.definition: The cochlea is the sense organ for hearing that converts sound energy to neural impulses.

concepts.name: outer ear
concepts.definition: The outer ear is one of the parts of the human hearing system that the lecture will begin with.

concepts.name: inner ear
concepts.definition: The inner ear is the final part of the hearing system that houses the cochlea.

concepts.name: Neural impulses
concepts.definition: Neural impulses are the signals that sound waves are converted into through the mechanisms of the ear.

concepts.name: Middle ear
concepts.definition: The middle ear is one of the three parts of the ear.

concepts.name: Sound perception
concepts.definition: This is the process by which we perceive sound, which occurs at three levels.

concepts.name: Social level
concepts.definition: This perception helps us carry out social interactions with other individuals.

concepts.name: Psychophysics
concepts.definition: Psychophysics is the scientific study of perceptual phenomena that are produced by physical stimuli.

concepts.name: Psychoacoustics
concepts.definition: Psychoacoustics is a more specific area of psychophysics where the term physical is replaced with the term acoustic, studying phenomena produced by acoustic stimuli or sound.

concepts.name: Weber's law
concepts.definition: Weber's law is a law that captures Just noticeable difference, represented as delta M by M equals C.

concepts.name: Stevens' Power Law
concepts.definition: Stevens' Power Law, represented by P = C * m to the power x, implies that if the exponent is less than 1, a large increase in physical stimulus results in only a moderate increase in perceived loudness.

concepts.name: Just Noticeable Difference
concepts.definition: This is the threshold change required for a change to be perceived, or the range below which a change is not perceived.

concepts.name: Auditory Perception
concepts.definition: This refers to our perception when physical stimuli are replaced with acoustic stimuli.

concepts.name: Pitch perception
concepts.definition: Pitch perception is the ability to perceive the frequency of a sound wave.

concepts.name: Localization
concepts.definition: Localization deals with estimating the location of a sound source by hearing it.

concepts.name: Azimuth
concepts.definition: This is the angle in the horizontal plane between the forward direction and the source of the sound.

concepts.name: Elevation
concepts.definition: This is the angle between the actual source direction and the horizontal plane.

concepts.name: Radius
concepts.definition: The source is called the radius, which is the distance from the origin (the human head) to the source.

concepts.name: Head-related transfer functions
concepts.definition: HRTF models how we receive sound from a location in space.

concepts.name: Non-stationary
concepts.definition: Non-stationary means that the auditory component is moving with the user.

concepts.name: Interactive
concepts.definition: Interactive means that the auditory component is dependent on the listener's actions.

concepts.name: Binaural sound
concepts.definition: Binaural sound is synthesized using a pair of HRTF for both ears.

concepts.name: Proprioceptive sense or proprioception
concepts.definition: This is introduced as the sixth sense, alongside the five traditional senses.

concepts.name: Full immersive experience
concepts.definition: This is the context for the discussion regarding the role of senses other than visual and auditory.

concepts.name: Human visual perceptual system
