concepts.definition: This system's knowledge helps in building better XR systems.

concepts.name: Human auditory system
concepts.definition: This system helps create immersive experience in XR in addition to the visual perceptual system.

concepts.name: Touch sense
concepts.definition: The touch sense is a human sense related to the perception of touch and is supported by dedicated receptors.

concepts.name: Proprioception
concepts.definition: Proprioception is the awareness of the pose of each movable human body part, which is defined as awareness of movement.

concepts.name: Kinesthesis
concepts.definition: Kinesthesis provides information on velocities, acceleration, and forces while moving the body parts.

concepts.name: Somatosensory system
concepts.definition: The somatosensory system is a sensory organ that handles touch, proprioception, and kinesthesis.

concepts.name: Haptic perception
concepts.definition: Haptic perception is the perception of the overall geometric shape of objects.

concepts.name: Haptic exploration
concepts.definition: Haptic exploration involves object handling or manipulation to infer the overall geometric shape of an object.

concepts.name: Muscle spindles
concepts.definition: Muscle spindles are receptors embedded inside each muscle that report to the brain on changes in length.

concepts.name: Force feedback
concepts.definition: Force feedback is typically the most popular way of providing touch sensation stimuli as output and is quite common in many XR systems, particularly VR systems.

concepts.name: Haptic pin array
concepts.definition: A matrix of pins controlled by a computer that is forced upward to simulate various textures as a fingertip scans across its surface.

concepts.name: Tangible user interfaces
concepts.definition: Real-world objects that are used to provide touch sensation feedback, replacing computer-controlled haptic devices.

concepts.name: Chemical senses
concepts.definition: These senses are generally grouped together because the receptors work by chemical interaction with the molecules that arrive on them.

concepts.name: Taste/Smell
concepts.definition: Taste or smell is nothing but a chemical reaction of the chemoreceptors with the stimuli that are arriving to the receptors.

concepts.name: Smell interfaces
concepts.definition: Smell interfaces are devices meant for providing stimuli to our nose.

concepts.name: Olfactory displays
concepts.definition: This is a term used to call smell interfaces, which are generic displays designed to provide olfactory stimuli.

concepts.name: Taste interfaces
concepts.definition: These are systems, such as those using electrodes placed over and under the tongue, designed to simulate the main taste types.

concepts.name: Immersion
concepts.definition: Immersion is a state that can be increased in a VR or XR setting when appropriate support is provided.

concepts.name: XR systems
concepts.definition: XR systems are a class of interactive systems because the users of these systems are supposed to be laypersons.

concepts.name: Interactive system
concepts.definition: An interactive system is application software designed for laypersons who do not need to know how the hardware or software works.

concepts.name: Extended Reality Systems
concepts.definition: These are the specific type of interactive systems that the course is focusing on.

concepts.name: Usability
concepts.definition: Usability is always discussed in relation to a specific group of users, a specified context of use, and specific tasks.

concepts.name: User-centric software
concepts.definition: User-centric software is designed to be usable systems that cater to the needs and expectations of laypersons.

concepts.name: Software development life cycle
concepts.definition: It is followed to develop and deploy software so as to comprehensively capture and represent the design and development activities that should go into building the software.

concepts.name: Software engineering
concepts.definition: It is a single term used to represent the idea of software development life cycle, or engineering a software.

concepts.name: Stages
concepts.definition: They capture or structure the whole process and through their connection, they essentially let us represent in a very structured manner how the development process should take place.

concepts.name: design space
concepts.definition: The set of all possible designs.

concepts.name: Highly iterative lifecycle
concepts.definition: A highly iterative lifecycle is required to implement a user-centric design approach for building interactive software, allowing for frequent looping to account for user feedback.

concepts.name: Design prototype evaluate cycle
concepts.definition: This cycle comprises the design stage, prototyping stage, and early evaluation stage.

concepts.name: Code testing
concepts.definition: Testing that ensures there are no bugs and the code executes properly.

concepts.name: Requirement gathering stage
concepts.definition: The requirement gathering stage involves involving the end users along with the customer or client of the system.

concepts.name: Interface design
concepts.definition: This is one of the two parts of designing the system within the design-prototype-evaluate cycle, focusing on the user's point of view.

concepts.name: Code design
concepts.definition: This is a design part that is separate from the design-prototype-evaluate cycle and deals with coding.

concepts.name: Requirement analysis
concepts.definition: When referring to requirement analysis, it typically refers to the requirements of the client.

concepts.name: Early evaluation
concepts.definition: Evaluating the ideas of interface and interaction design quickly with fewer resources and less time.

concepts.name: Empirical study
concepts.definition: A stage required to ensure the product conforms to usability, which involves systematic testing with the end users.

concepts.name: Interactive System Development Lifecycle
concepts.definition: It is the overall idea of what should be done to build interactive systems which are usable.

concepts.name: Usable System
concepts.definition: It is the desired outcome of the overall process of building interactive systems.

concepts.name: Case study
concepts.definition: A practical system used to understand different aspects of system development.

concepts.name: Digital preservation of physical heritage
concepts.definition: The process of preserving the heritage of the Majuli River Island in the digital space.

concepts.name: Virtual reality system
concepts.definition: A system used to digitally preserve the Majuli River Islands' ecological and cultural heritage.

concepts.name: Tangible heritage
concepts.definition: Tangible heritage aspects refer to heritage aspects of the island which someone can touch and feel, such as cultural artifacts or architectural aspects.

concepts.name: Intangible heritage
concepts.definition: Intangible heritage aspects cannot be touched and felt, but they can be sensed through different means, including traditional skills and knowledge.

concepts.name: Cultural heritage
concepts.definition: Cultural heritage consists of two broad aspects: tangible heritage and intangible heritage.

concepts.name: Integration of man and nature
concepts.definition: The island's unique position led to a distinctive integration of man and nature.

concepts.name: ecological heritage
concepts.definition: This refers to the flora and fauna of the island which exist due to its unique geology, geography, and topography.

concepts.name: digital preservation
concepts.definition: This is the necessary action taken because the island is constantly being hit by severe annual floods and erosion, which threatens its existence.

concepts.name: erosion
concepts.definition: Erosion is the process where the island is slowly consumed by the river, reducing the habitable area.

concepts.name: Digital heritage preservation
concepts.definition: It is the process of using digital media to preserve heritage, which can be cultural, educational, scientific, or ecological.

concepts.name: Archiving
concepts.definition: Archiving means storing the visual and audio files that capture the information heritage of a particular entity, object, space, or place.

concepts.name: Heritage preservation
concepts.definition: Heritage preservation involves creating an archive of heritage information which ideally should be in the form of multimedia comprising images, videos, audios, and texts.

concepts.name: Experiencing the heritage
concepts.definition: Experiencing the heritage refers to a virtual tour or an exploration of the island utilizing the archival information.

concepts.name: Archive of heritage information
concepts.definition: The archive of heritage information is created during heritage preservation and comprises multimedia such as images, videos, audios, and texts.

concepts.name: Use case
concepts.definition: A use case covers what it is all about and why it needs to be done.

concepts.name: Immersive virtual tours
concepts.definition: These are experiences through which the heritage is experienced, forming one component of the digital heritage preservation system.

concepts.name: Satras
concepts.definition: These are Vaishnavite monasteries that serve as centers of religious significance and cultural vitality on the island.

concepts.name: Hot spots
concepts.definition: These are specific points created on a map of the island where the tangible and intangible aspects of the cultural landscape are captured.

concepts.name: Multimodal archive
concepts.definition: This is the archive created to preserve the heritage aspects of the island, utilizing various data types like images, videos, and textual descriptions.

concepts.name: Usability testing
concepts.definition: Testing that focuses on how well a system works for the user, rather than only testing the code.

concepts.name: Tangible and intangible heritage
concepts.definition: The vast information, both physical and non-physical, that is being preserved and explored in the virtual tour.

concepts.name: System-Centered Design
concepts.definition: System-centered design is an approach where the development is driven by the skill and interest of the developer rather than the needs and expectations of the user.

concepts.name: Requirement Gathering
concepts.definition: Requirement gathering is the process of following specific methods and processes to gather end user requirements, ensuring that the resulting design is usable.

concepts.name: Specification
concepts.definition: Something that is required for system implementation.

concepts.name: Usability requirements
concepts.definition: Sentence is an introductory statement that signals the upcoming discussion of what usability requirements mean, but it does not provide a definition itself.

concepts.name: End user requirements
concepts.definition: Requirements specific to the end user, as opposed to client requirements.

concepts.name: Requirement
concepts.definition: In this context, the term requirement specifically refers to end user requirements.

concepts.name: Feasibility
concepts.definition: These are requirements related to the first stage, such as deciding on mobile platforms or programming languages.

concepts.name: Code design stage
concepts.definition: This stage involves questions about how to store various information, such as whether to use RDBMS tools like MySQL.

concepts.name: System specification
concepts.definition: This is the outcome that requirements lead to.

concepts.name: usability
concepts.definition: Usability is the extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction in a specified context of use.

concepts.name: Functional requirements
concepts.definition: These are system features and abilities of the system to carry out tasks in terms of some functions which are treated as black boxes.

concepts.name: Quality attributes
concepts.definition: These are characteristics that usability requirements are typically related to.

concepts.name: interface issues
concepts.definition: Interface issues refer to the design or qualities of the interface that should be usable, making the interface usable.

concepts.name: external system interface
concepts.definition: The external system interface involves hardware and software interfacing, as well as the interfacing between the hardware and software.

concepts.name: user interface
concepts.definition: The user interface is the area where usability issues come into the picture.

concepts.name: requirement gathering methods
concepts.definition: Requirement gathering methods are the techniques that can be deployed to gather requirements and ensure usability.

concepts.name: Contextual inquiry
concepts.definition: A requirement gathering method that gathers end user requirements by observing users in their natural work setting.

concepts.name: Natural work setting
concepts.definition: The specified context where users are observed performing tasks to gather requirements.

concepts.name: Semi-structured interview process
concepts.definition: A method of contextual inquiry that consists of both interviews and observations.

concepts.name: Usability requirement gathering
concepts.definition: An essential part of ensuring a usable design, which allows for a proper design that takes care of users' needs and expectations.

concepts.name: Contextual inquiry
concepts.definition: Contextual inquiry is a method used to observe targeted groups of users in their natural work setting to understand how they behave and what they do.

concepts.name: Passive mode
concepts.definition: In passive mode, user activities are recorded or videotaped, and the activities are then observed later by the observer.

concepts.name: Master apprentice model
concepts.definition: The master apprentice model requires the observer to act as an apprentice and treat the users as masters during the inquiry.

concepts.name: Reflect
concepts.definition: Reflect means analyzing the data.

concepts.name: Execute stage
concepts.definition: This is the stage where the actual inquiry takes place.

concepts.name: Initiate stage
concepts.definition: This stage requires contacting authorities for necessary permissions and opening communication with end users.

concepts.name: Execute test stage
concepts.definition: This stage is where the actual observation is performed and data is recorded.

concepts.name: Close stage
concepts.definition: This stage involves formally closing the activity, ideally by sending thank you notes to the users.

concepts.name: Reflect stage
concepts.definition: In this stage, the observer or experimental team analyzes the collected data and identifies the design goals.

concepts.name: Design goals
concepts.definition: These are the objectives that are identified by analyzing the data collected during the execute stage.

concepts.name: Affinity diagram method
concepts.definition: This is a technique used to arrange data to easily find patterns, which then leads to the design specification of the design goals.

concepts.name: Data
concepts.definition: The data is essentially the notes taken by the observers while observing the behavior.

concepts.name: Idea
concepts.definition: An idea is called a note when following the affinity diagram.

concepts.name: Physical note-taking
concepts.definition: This is the traditional method of taking notes, typically done on pen and paper.

concepts.name: Generate and display the ideas
concepts.definition: This refers to the combined process of generating ideas and then showing those ideas, as part of the affinity diagram method.

concepts.name: Groups
concepts.definition: Groups are formed by identifying patterns among ideas so that similar ideas with similar patterns can be sorted into a single group.

concepts.name: Sorting of the ideas into groups
concepts.definition: This is the stage where ideas are sorted into groups by identifying patterns among them so that similar ideas can be grouped together.

concepts.name: Content management
concepts.definition: Content management is a common idea that relates issues such as content relocation not being possible and erasing content being a daunting task.

concepts.name: Header
concepts.definition: A header is a name provided for the pattern which binds multiple ideas together.

concepts.name: Idea generation
concepts.definition: Idea generation refers to the final note that is taken by the observer.

concepts.name: Display
concepts.definition: The display is the place where the notes are put together, which can be a wall or a board.

concepts.name: Final drawing
concepts.definition: The final drawing is essentially sorting all the ideas into groups.

concepts.name: Design Recommendation
concepts.definition: Design recommendations are a set of suggestions that can be developed based on the collected data.

concepts.name: Informed design choice
concepts.definition: An informed design choice is one where the information used comes through methods like contextual inquiry, ensuring user needs and expectations are met.

concepts.name: Prescription for implementation
concepts.definition: A prescription for implementation is not the requirement, as it specifies how to implement the requirement.

concepts.name: Contextual inquiry
concepts.definition: This is a usability requirement gathering method that the discussion has started.

concepts.name: Requirement gathering
concepts.definition: This is the process of gathering usability requirements for the users and the tour.

concepts.name: Guidelines
concepts.definition: Guidelines are framed based on observations to suggest what the app should do or should not do.

concepts.name: Software requirements specification
concepts.definition: The Software Requirements Specification (SRS) is a document used for specifying all types of requirements, including both functional and non-functional.

concepts.name: Functional requirement specification
concepts.definition: This is the formal representation or specification of requirements within the SRS document.

concepts.name: Know the user
concepts.definition: This is the first stage of the process, which involves understanding the target audience.

concepts.name: Functional specifications
concepts.definition: Functional specifications are one possible outcome of utilizing the result of the analysis, alongside guidelines.

concepts.name: Data subset
concepts.definition: A limited portion of the total data that is made accessible to each specific group of users.

concepts.name: Design challenges
concepts.definition: Design challenges are key issues that the development process sought to address.

concepts.name: Location awareness
concepts.definition: It is the crucial process of ensuring users have accurate location information to prevent disorientation, especially when dealing with large geographies.

concepts.name: Tangible and intangible heritage experience
concepts.definition: This refers to the required provision of both tangible and intangible heritage experiences to the user.

concepts.name: Interaction aid for enhanced user experience
concepts.definition: This challenge involves providing support that includes navigation support, user-friendly interfaces, and increasing presence through natural interactions.

concepts.name: Design language
concepts.definition: A design language is required to express our design.

concepts.name: Interface and interaction design
concepts.definition: When discussing the design of interface and interaction, there are two issues to consider.

concepts.name: Creative thinking process
concepts.definition: This is a process where design can start by relying on creativity, which may be aided by intuition, experience, or domain knowledge.

concepts.name: Heuristics
concepts.definition: Heuristics are guidelines, often referred to alongside checklists and thumb rules, that can be used as a starting point for the design process.

concepts.name: Prototype
concepts.definition: A prototype can be thought of as a language to express design ideas and can be considered a language for interface design.

concepts.name: Generic guidelines
concepts.definition: These guidelines are very broad in nature, small in size, and cover broad aspects of interactive systems at a high level.

concepts.name: Specification of design
concepts.definition: This essentially refers to the language used to express whatever we are thinking about the design.

concepts.name: Specific guideline set
concepts.definition: A specific guideline set consists of rules applicable to a particular system or domain, such as VR or immersive systems.

concepts.name: Consistency
concepts.definition: Consistency is a fundamental principle that must be actively strived for when designing any system or interface.

concepts.name: Internal consistency
concepts.definition: The practice of utilizing the same elements and interactions for the same tasks across different parts of the design.

concepts.name: External consistency
concepts.definition: The principle that the system's elements and interactions should closely match the user's real-world knowledge and experience.

concepts.name: Hotkeys
concepts.definition: Hotkeys are a combination of keys used to perform an action, such as saving a document.

concepts.name: Universal usability
concepts.definition: Universal usability is the design principle that requires facilities for all classes of users.

concepts.name: Informative feedback
concepts.definition: Informative feedback is the required response given to the user for whatever action they perform.

concepts.name: Progress bar
concepts.definition: A visual element that appears to show the percentage of tasks completed during an operation.

concepts.name: Usable design
concepts.definition: A design quality where the user can understand what the system is doing, whether a task is getting done, and how much of the task is completed.

concepts.name: Storage metaphor
concepts.definition: A representation, such as a floppy disk icon, used to represent the concept of storage.

concepts.name: Design dialogues to yield closure
concepts.definition: Designing the system so that the user feels the task is started, executed, and finally completed.

concepts.name: Beginning part, middle part, and an end part
concepts.definition: It is a design structure that organizes activities or task execution into distinct phases: a beginning part, a middle part, and a completion or end part.

concepts.name: Error prevention and simple error handling
concepts.definition: Error prevention and simple error handling (Rule 5) requires offering error prevention in the design, along with mechanisms to handle errors if they occur.

concepts.name: Reversal of action
concepts.definition: This is a design objective that allows users to return from an erroneous situation after making a mistake.

concepts.name: Keeping the users in control
concepts.definition: Keeping the users in control means letting the users feel that they are in control of the system.

concepts.name: Perceive their interaction
concepts.definition: Users should be able to understand and perceive that something is happening, which signifies a change in system state.

concepts.name: Feedback
concepts.definition: Feedback requires that both the actions taken and the resulting outcomes of those actions are provided.

concepts.name: Short term memory
concepts.definition: It is a kind of notes or non-permanent storage used to aid day-to-day activities.

concepts.name: Long term memory
concepts.definition: This is permanent storage from which information is brought into short-term memory to aid activities.

concepts.name: 7 plus or minus 2 rule
concepts.definition: This rule states that it is best to keep between 5 to 9 chunks of information in short-term memory at one time.

concepts.name: Chunk of information
concepts.definition: This refers to a unit of information that should ideally be kept between 5 to 9 for optimum user outcome.

concepts.name: Reduce short term memory load
concepts.definition: Reduce short term memory load is presented as the final rule in the discussion of system design principles.

concepts.name: Object interaction
concepts.definition: The selection and manipulation of objects that are part of the virtual environment.

concepts.name: Navigation
concepts.definition: The act of moving from one point to another within the virtual environment.

concepts.name: Interaction for system control
concepts.definition: System-related settings interaction required to change those settings.

concepts.name: Interaction for selection
concepts.definition: This type of interaction involves selecting the object with which the user wants to interact.

concepts.name: Interaction for manipulation
concepts.definition: This interaction occurs after selection and changes the properties of the object.

concepts.name: Object selection
concepts.definition: This refers to specifying one or more objects from a set of virtual objects that are part of the virtual world.

concepts.name: Target occlusion
concepts.definition: Target occlusion is the condition where a target object is hidden, either partially or fully, by other surrounding objects.

concepts.name: Hand selection
concepts.definition: This is a method where the user uses their hand to select objects in a virtual world.

concepts.name: Pointing-based selection
concepts.definition: This is a method used to select objects in a virtual world.

concepts.name: Image plane selection
concepts.definition: This technique involves the user holding one or two hands between the eye and the desired object, and then providing a signal to select the object when it lines up with the hand and eye.

concepts.name: Hand selection technique
concepts.definition: This technique involves selecting virtual objects in the virtual world using the hand.

concepts.name: Virtual hand
concepts.definition: It is an avatar of the physical hand that is visible in the virtual world.

concepts.name: Go-go technique
concepts.definition: This technique allows the user to interactively change the virtual arm length to select distant objects without tiring.

concepts.name: Prism
concepts.definition: This is an improvement of the go-go technique that applies scaled-down motion to the virtual hand when the user's hand is moving below a specified speed.

concepts.name: Intent-driven selection
concepts.definition: This technique uses gestures or the posture of the virtual fingers as an indication of the user's level of confidence in selecting an object.

concepts.name: Proximity spheres
concepts.definition: These spheres are used to progressively refine the selection of an object based on hand postures.

concepts.name: Ray casting
concepts.definition: A basic technique where the user points at objects with a virtual ray.

concepts.name: Bend cast
concepts.definition: A technique where the system bends the ray towards the object closest to the path.

concepts.name: Depth ray
concepts.definition: An improvement over the basic ray casting method used to disambiguate between objects when the pointing vector hits multiple targets.

concepts.name: Hand pointing
concepts.definition: Pointing done using the hand or handheld input devices.

concepts.name: Eye gaze pointing
concepts.definition: Extending the ray using eye gaze controlling devices or eye trackers, changing pointing with eye gaze.

concepts.name: Volumetric selection
concepts.definition: This technique enables the user to select a 3D region in space, which then selects corresponding objects within that space.

concepts.name: Head crusher technique
concepts.definition: The user positions the thumb and the forefinger around the desired object such that the object is enclosed by the thumb and forefinger in the 2D image plane.

concepts.name: Cone casting flashlight technique
concepts.definition: A cone is cast to a distance, and objects within the cone get selected, extending the ray casting idea.

concepts.name: Sphere casting flashlight technique
concepts.definition: A sphere is cast onto the nearest intersected surface, and the objects found within the sphere are selected.

concepts.name: Two-handed box selection technique
concepts.definition: The user uses both hands to position, orient, and shape a box or a cube to select a specified region of the 3D space.

concepts.name: Manipulation
concepts.definition: Manipulation is the process of modifying an object's properties, such as position, orientation, scale, shape, color, texture, or behavior.

concepts.name: Hand manipulation
concepts.definition: Hand manipulation uses a virtual hand, smart gloves, gesture-based manipulation, or controller-based interaction to manipulate objects.

concepts.name: Indirect manipulation
concepts.definition: Indirect manipulation involves manipulating other objects that are mapped to the desired virtual object, thereby manipulating the desired object without direct interaction.

concepts.name: World in miniature
concepts.definition: World in miniature (WIM) provides the user a miniature handheld model of the virtual environment, allowing indirect manipulation of virtual objects.

concepts.name: Locomotion
concepts.definition: Locomotion is the travel part of navigation, which is the motor component of navigation.

concepts.name: Exploration
concepts.definition: Exploration is a type of travel where there is no explicit goal to reach, and the user simply wants to move around to see or learn things.

concepts.name: Search
concepts.definition: Search involves searching for or moving to a specified target location.

concepts.name: Locomotion techniques
concepts.definition: These are the four broad types of techniques used to accomplish travel from one point to another.

concepts.name: Walking-based locomotion
concepts.definition: Traveling in the virtual world by physically walking in the physical world or the real world.

concepts.name: Partial gait technique
concepts.definition: A technique where the user walks but remains in the same physical place, and the walking pattern is mapped to different types of walking in the virtual space.

concepts.name: Gait negation technique
concepts.definition: A technique where specialized setup cancels the user's lateral movements while keeping their physical position fixed, allowing movement to be mapped to a specific virtual movement.

concepts.name: steering-based navigation
concepts.definition: This category indicates continuous control of direction and speed while the user is moving from one point to another.

concepts.name: spatial steering-based navigation
concepts.definition: In this case, the navigation is controlled using the user's body parts.

concepts.name: physical steering-based locomotion technique
concepts.definition: This technique involves some physical setups and separate hardware, such as bike locomotion platforms or VR simulators.

concepts.name: selection-based navigation
concepts.definition: This technique allows users to focus on where to go rather than how to get there.

concepts.name: target selection-based locomotion
concepts.definition: In this technique, the user selects the destination or target where they want to move, and the virtual viewpoint changes.

concepts.name: manipulation-based locomotion techniques
concepts.definition: Locomotion works by manipulating the user's position, orientation, or scale using gestures that control either the virtual viewpoint or the virtual world.

concepts.name: Wayfinding
concepts.definition: Wayfinding refers to location awareness and ascertaining a path through the environment to the desired destination.

concepts.name: Cognitive map
concepts.definition: A cognitive map is a mental model or map of the surroundings and overall environment.

concepts.name: Mental model
concepts.definition: A mental model is essentially a cognitive map of the surroundings and overall environment.

concepts.name: Landmark knowledge
concepts.definition: Landmark knowledge is knowledge about landmarks in surroundings or other places.

concepts.name: Procedural knowledge
concepts.definition: Procedural knowledge is the sequence of actions required to follow a path.

concepts.name: Topological knowledge
concepts.definition: Topological knowledge is the overall map-like knowledge of the environment.

concepts.name: Wayfinding support
concepts.definition: Wayfinding support is required for a system to provide a good immersive user experience, ensuring travel supports are effectively used while performing navigation.

concepts.name: Landmark
concepts.definition: A landmark is any obvious distinct non-mobile object that is positioned in a given place and can be seen from several locations.

concepts.name: Path following
concepts.definition: Path following is a wayfinding support where multiple paths through a single space may be denoted by colors so that the user knows there are different paths to reach a destination.

concepts.name: Breadcrumbs
concepts.definition: Breadcrumbs is a support that involves leaving a trail of the path followed by predecessors, allowing users to know when they have been somewhere before.

concepts.name: multimodal interaction techniques for system control
concepts.definition: These techniques involve combining multiple interaction methods, such as combining voice with gestures.

concepts.name: navigation interaction
concepts.definition: Navigation interaction comprises the processes of travel and wayfinding.

concepts.name: Enhance the user's presence
concepts.definition: This objective is to ensure that the users feel immersed and present within the virtual environment.

concepts.name: Minimize cyber sickness
concepts.definition: This objective was to design the tour to be comfortable and to minimize any risk of cyber sickness.

concepts.name: Interactive system development lifecycle model
concepts.definition: This model involves continuously refining design ideas based on feedback and observations by involving the end users.

concepts.name: Distinct categories
concepts.definition: These are groups of users that each possess their own unique preferences for visiting or exploring the island.

concepts.name: Contextual inquiry methods
concepts.definition: These methods are used to collect specific preferences from users to tailor the content and features of the virtual tour.

concepts.name: Points of interest
concepts.definition: These are the specific locations on the island, such as satras, villages, and towns, that are marked and need to be covered by the tour.

concepts.name: curved screen
concepts.definition: A design element that shows content in an immersive setting.

concepts.name: immersive setting
concepts.definition: A setting where the screen is curved and shows content to the user.

concepts.name: boat ride experience
concepts.definition: An element added to give the user the feeling of being transported from one bank of the river to the other.

concepts.name: 360-degree boat ride video
concepts.definition: The method used to give the user the feeling of actually traveling through a boat.

concepts.name: user group
concepts.definition: A category of users, such as pilgrims, students, or tourists, that the user can choose before the experience begins.

concepts.name: Pre-processing
concepts.definition: Pre-processing is the initial processing of collected content, such as images and videos, to improve the visual appearance and user experience.

concepts.name: Uniform illumination
concepts.definition: Uniform illumination is the process of editing images and videos to ensure that the same illumination effect is present across all images, regardless of when they were taken.

concepts.name: 360-degree images
concepts.definition: 360-degree images are images used to create scenes where the user is traveling from one image to another.

concepts.name: Virtual tablet
concepts.definition: The virtual tablet acts as the main interface, providing navigation tools, a video player, and access to information content.

concepts.name: Interactive tablet interface
concepts.definition: This is a provided interface that users utilize for interaction and navigation.

concepts.name: Video player
concepts.definition: A component integrated into the tablet interface that allows users to access cultural and ecological videos relevant to their current location in the virtual world.

concepts.name: Minimap concept
concepts.definition: The minimap concept is useful to provide a sense of belonging or sense of orientation to a place.

concepts.name: World-in-miniature type of map
concepts.definition: This type of map provides a miniature representation of the entire island or a specific place on the island.

concepts.name: Dual maps
concepts.definition: Dual maps consist of a global map and a local map, which are used to reduce clutter and provide clear navigation support.

concepts.name: Dynamic orientation awareness
concepts.definition: This feature provides users with spatial orientation, helping them know in which direction to move.

concepts.name: Tablet interface
concepts.definition: The interface that includes the video player and allows users to access cultural and ecological videos relevant to the current user location.

concepts.name: View interpolation technique
concepts.definition: A technique that blurs the boundaries between two images to ensure a smooth feeling of transitioning from one image to another.

concepts.name: Virtual vehicle metaphor
concepts.definition: A 3D model of a vehicle that facilitates long-distance travel within the tour.

concepts.name: Selection-based locomotion technique
concepts.definition: A technique where the user selects a destination using pre-planned routes, rather than instantaneous movement.

concepts.name: Ray casting interactions
concepts.definition: An interaction method that allows the user to operate the vehicle and provide direction of movement.

concepts.name: Informative notifications and descriptions
concepts.definition: Elements that provide additional context about locations and significant spots, enriching the user's understanding and engagement.

concepts.name: Directional arrows
concepts.definition: Elements added to make the user aware of points of interest by guiding them on which way to move.

concepts.name: Information icons
concepts.definition: Icons that provide further details about a place upon interaction, usually in the form of textual information.

concepts.name: Controlled navigation technique
concepts.definition: A technique where users can navigate or teleport using a joystick, which reduces abrupt movements that can cause discomfort.

concepts.name: Design
concepts.definition: In this context, design refers to interface and interaction design, not the code design.

concepts.name: Consistent visual cues
concepts.definition: Consistent visual cues are design elements that were implemented in the system.

concepts.name: Smooth transitions
concepts.definition: These transitions are implemented in the design to help maintain spatial orientation and reduce sensory conflicts.

concepts.name: Implementation
concepts.definition: Implementation refers to the process of how to implement an XR system.

concepts.name: User requirement gathering
concepts.definition: User requirement gathering is the process of how to gather requirements.

concepts.name: Empirical or usability evaluation
concepts.definition: This is the evaluation of the whole system from the point of view of usability.

concepts.name: Requirement gathering analysis and specification stage
concepts.definition: This is a stage in the development lifecycle that follows the feasibility study.

concepts.name: Prototyping and early evaluation
concepts.definition: This is the primary focus of the lecture, involving the quick modeling and testing of design ideas early in the development process.

concepts.name: Usability evaluation
concepts.definition: This is the process of testing design ideas to ensure that when implemented, they lead to a usable system.

concepts.name: Experience design
concepts.definition: This involves the entire design-prototype-evaluate cycle, where the process is iterative, requiring many cycles before the design is stabilized.

concepts.name: Quick usability evaluation technique
concepts.definition: This is a technique required to quickly evaluate the usability of design ideas so that many cycles can be accommodated within a reasonable timeframe.

concepts.name: Prototype
concepts.definition: A model of an idea that should be able to be built quickly to demonstrate the concept.

concepts.name: Horizontal prototypes
concepts.definition: These prototypes depict the entire interface at a surface level, showing how the interface appears to the user without providing any functionality or interaction.

concepts.name: Vertical prototypes
concepts.definition: These prototypes are designed to represent interactions or functionalities, implementing selected features in depth from the first screen to the last.

concepts.name: Low-fidelity prototypes
concepts.definition: These are prototypes created without technological intervention, meaning they do not require writing any program, code, or even a computer, and are often made with paper or cardboard.

concepts.name: Interface sketches
concepts.definition: These are drawings that depict major components of an interface and provide a simple illustration to envision the appearance of the interface.

concepts.name: Storyboarding
concepts.definition: Storyboarding is a series of sketches used to represent interaction, often modifying the basic prototyping approach.

concepts.name: Keyframe
concepts.definition: A keyframe is a snapshot of the interaction at a particular point in time, representing a sketch in a storyboard.

concepts.name: Low fidelity approach
concepts.definition: This is an approach where no computer is required, and the storyboard can be done on a simple paper without using any digital medium.

concepts.name: Medium fidelity approach
concepts.definition: This approach uses a computer to create simple prototypes, which are typically of low fidelity.

concepts.name: High fidelity approach
concepts.definition: This approach involves creating prototypes with computer programs, which is effectively actual software development on a reduced scale.

concepts.name: Wizard of Oz approach
concepts.definition: It is a prototyping method where a human subject interacts with a system they believe is autonomous, but the system is actually operated by an unseen human.

concepts.name: Wizard
concepts.definition: The wizard is the unseen human operator who controls the computer and returns the results to the subject.

concepts.name: throwaway prototypes
concepts.definition: These are prototypes that are used for a quick evaluation and then discarded after use.

concepts.name: incremental prototypes
concepts.definition: In this approach, the system is designed into units or modules, each of which is separately prototyped, tested, and then integrated into the overall system.

concepts.name: evolutionary prototypes
concepts.definition: These prototypes start with a simpler version of the system, which is tested and refined, and then evolves into the full system by adding more functionalities.

concepts.name: Expert evaluation
concepts.definition: This quick evaluation technique is used to evaluate prototypes without spending too much time or resources.

concepts.name: Quick evaluation
concepts.definition: This technique is used for quick and cheap evaluation, typically performed at an early stage of the design process.

concepts.name: Cognitive walkthrough
concepts.definition: It is a usability inspection method used to identify usability problems by inspecting a prototype.

concepts.name: Usability inspection method
concepts.definition: This is a technique where usability problems are identified by inspecting the prototype.

concepts.name: Storyboard
concepts.definition: Each prototype is a storyboard, which is a series of sketches depicting changes of screen after each interaction.

concepts.name: Interface-level tasks
concepts.definition: These are the specific things that need to be done to identify or find out information from the calendar app.

concepts.name: Heuristic evaluation technique
concepts.definition: The heuristic evaluation technique involves evaluators checking a prototype against a checklist of heuristics, reporting whether each is followed or violated, and then compiling the reports to identify major usability issues.

concepts.name: Nielsen's 10 heuristics
concepts.definition: Nielsen's 10 heuristics is one example of a general set of heuristics.

concepts.name: Visibility of system status
concepts.definition: This heuristic concerns how visible the status of the system is to the user.

concepts.name: User evaluation
concepts.definition: A quick evaluation technique that involves users to get feedback by asking them questions directly.

concepts.name: Evaluation with self-reports
concepts.definition: A method where user feedback is collected using rating scales.

concepts.name: Subjective or preference data
concepts.definition: Data collected from users using rating scales.

concepts.name: Post-task questionnaire
concepts.definition: A questionnaire used to collect feedback after a user performs a specific task on the prototype.

concepts.name: Post-session questionnaire
concepts.definition: A questionnaire administered at the end of a session after all tasks have been completed.

concepts.name: System Usability Scale
concepts.definition: A post-session questionnaire consisting of 10 statements used to obtain an overall usability score.

concepts.name: ASQ, SUS
concepts.definition: These are generic questionnaires applicable to any interactive system, not specifically meant for extended reality systems.

concepts.name: Simulator sickness questionnaire
concepts.definition: The Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ) is the most extensively used questionnaire among those designed for cyber sickness.

concepts.name: Virtual reality sickness questionnaire
concepts.definition: This questionnaire is good for evaluating VR experiences with HMDs.

concepts.name: Misery scale
concepts.definition: This is a shorter and more precise questionnaire used to assess specific conditions.

concepts.name: Full scale system implementation
concepts.definition: This is the next stage after design considerations, prototype building, and expert evaluations.

concepts.name: Cloud services
concepts.definition: Cloud services were used to store all videos, allowing them to be loaded from the cloud when a user clicks on a video thumbnail rather than being stored permanently on the client device.

concepts.name: Compressed images
concepts.definition: High-resolution 360 degree or 2D images were compressed to reduce the overall storage requirements of the application.

concepts.name: XR toolkit
concepts.definition: This toolkit was employed specifically for the Oculus Quest version of the application.

concepts.name: Google VR SDK
concepts.definition: This SDK was employed for the Cardboard version of the application.

concepts.name: ray casting-based selection method
concepts.definition: This method allows the user to make selections on the start screen by interacting with the displayed elements.

concepts.name: 360-degree video
concepts.definition: This is a video captured during field trips and is used to give the user the experience of traveling, such as by boat.

concepts.name: texture
concepts.definition: Texture is used from real images to create a realistic-looking appearance on the 3D models.

concepts.name: Empirical evaluation
concepts.definition: It is a stage that deals with evaluating the usability of the developed system with end users.

concepts.name: Empirical study
concepts.definition: This is the term used to refer to the stage of evaluation, which can also be called usability study or empirical research.

concepts.name: Controlled experiment
concepts.definition: A controlled experiment is performed to collect user behavioral data and analyze that data to reach a conclusion about usability.

concepts.name: Usability study
concepts.definition: In this context, it is a controlled experiment specifically related to usability evaluation.

concepts.name: Identification of research questions
concepts.definition: This is the first stage of the process, where questions are formulated for which answers are sought.

concepts.name: Determination of variables
concepts.definition: This is the second stage of the process, where variables are identified after the research questions have been formulated.

concepts.name: Design of experiment
concepts.definition: This is the third stage, which involves designing the experiment and collecting data by executing the experimental design.

concepts.name: Analysis of the data
concepts.definition: This is the fourth stage, which is a rigorous process used to scientifically and objectively conclude the overall usability aspects of the system.

concepts.name: Research question
concepts.definition: A question that guides an experiment, which is answered by collecting and analyzing empirical data.

concepts.name: Testable question
concepts.definition: A question that allows for the collection of objective data through a controlled study.

concepts.name: Non-testable question
concepts.definition: A question that cannot be set up for a controlled experiment to collect objective data.

concepts.name: Objective data
concepts.definition: Data collected through a controlled experiment or metric, rather than relying on subjective user interpretation or feedback.

concepts.name: Subjective interpretation
concepts.definition: Subjective interpretation refers to feedback based on users' personal interpretation, which makes it problematic for drawing a definitive conclusion.

concepts.name: Interface
concepts.definition: Interface is a variable where we assign the values: our interface versus MS Word interface.

concepts.name: Independent variable
concepts.definition: Independent variables are variables that are controlled.

concepts.name: Factors
concepts.definition: The term 'factors' is used to denote variables that are controlled.

concepts.name: Levels
concepts.definition: Levels are the values assigned to a variable, independent variable, or factor.

concepts.name: Test conditions
concepts.definition: The factors combined with their levels give us the test conditions for the experiment.

concepts.name: Dependent variable
concepts.definition: The dependent variable is the variable whose value depends on the interface.

concepts.name: Empirical
concepts.definition: It means observation in the real world of real users.

concepts.name: Research question framing
concepts.definition: This is the process of framing multiple testable research questions so that conclusions can be drawn about broader, generalizable questions.

concepts.name: empirical study
concepts.definition: An empirical study generally involves conducting experiments, collecting data, and analyzing data to find answers to the questions that have been formulated.

concepts.name: untestable
concepts.definition: These are more generic forms of questions whose answers are relevant to a general conclusion on usability.

concepts.name: User profile
concepts.definition: The user is defined based on well-defined characteristics or entries, which are used to select participants in an experiment.

concepts.name: Homogeneous user group
concepts.definition: A user group where members generally refer to similar backgrounds, such as educational, socio-economic, or cultural backgrounds.

concepts.name: Heterogeneous group of users
concepts.definition: A group of users who do not have similarity in their backgrounds.

concepts.name: Number of participants
concepts.definition: To draw reliable conclusions from empirical data, it is generally assumed that between 12 and 25 participants should be used.

concepts.name: Representative tasks
concepts.definition: These are tasks that are most frequently or commonly used by the potential user group when the interface is deployed in practice.

concepts.name: Task performance data
concepts.definition: Task performance data is collected when users carry out tasks during an experiment, and this data is supposed to be mostly objective.

concepts.name: Profile
concepts.definition: This refers to choosing a proper subset of end users for the experiment.

concepts.name: within-subject design
concepts.definition: A study design where each participant performs tasks corresponding to all test conditions.

concepts.name: between-subjects
concepts.definition: A study design where tasks are distributed among participants such that not all participants perform all tasks corresponding to all test conditions.

concepts.name: practice effect
concepts.definition: The phenomenon where performance improves simply because the user is practicing, which makes it difficult to determine if the improvement is due to the interface or human nature.

concepts.name: Latin square design
concepts.definition: A systematic method of varying the sequence of tasks assigned to each participant.

concepts.name: confounding variable
concepts.definition: A variable that confuses the analysis, making it difficult to conclude whether performance improvement is due to the design or inherent human nature.

concepts.name: Data analysis
concepts.definition: Data analysis is the main purpose of stage 4, which involves determining what to do with the collected data.

concepts.name: Mean
concepts.definition: The mean is the average of a group of data items that constitutes the sample.

concepts.name: Statistical significance
concepts.definition: Statistical significance is a measure that can tell us whether the data is reliable or not.

concepts.name: Reliability
concepts.definition: Reliability refers to the quality of the data that must be known before drawing conclusions based on the data.

concepts.name: Statistical significance tests
concepts.definition: These tests are needed to confirm the reliability of observations by determining if a relative difference persists irrespective of changes in the experiment.

concepts.name: P value
concepts.definition: The P value essentially refers to the probability of obtaining the data by chance.

concepts.name: Parametric tests
concepts.definition: This is one group of statistical tests, contrasted with non-parametric tests.

concepts.name: Non-parametric tests
concepts.definition: This is the other group of statistical tests, contrasted with parametric tests.

concepts.name: Paired sample t-test
concepts.definition: This is a specific type of test used in the context of the example provided.

concepts.name: Empirical evaluation
concepts.definition: It is the usability evaluation of the end product, which requires a full-fledged system evaluated with the end user.

concepts.name: Quick evaluation of the prototype
concepts.definition: This is a stage of the design prototype evaluation cycle that is done after the prototype is implemented but not the full system.

concepts.name: Evaluation study of the VR tour
concepts.definition: The goal of the evaluation study is to measure various aspects of user engagement, presence, and comfort within the virtual environment.

concepts.name: Empirical study
concepts.definition: An empirical study is collecting data from end users by the means of a controlled experiment where we make use of questionnaires for collection of data.

concepts.name: Presence questionnaire
concepts.definition: The presence questionnaire is a standard questionnaire used to measure presence.

concepts.name: User groups
concepts.definition: User groups were divided into three categories corresponding to pilgrims, students, and tourists.

concepts.name: Likert scale
concepts.definition: A Likert scale is a rating scale used to record participant responses, such as the one ranging from 1 to 7.

concepts.name: Simulator sickness questionnaire
concepts.definition: A standard questionnaire (SSQ) used for measuring cyber sickness in the context of immersive experiences.

concepts.name: Previous presence questionnaire
concepts.definition: The Previous Presence Questionnaire (QEP) utilized a rating scale of 1 to 7, which is a Likert scale.

concepts.name: Familiarity bias
concepts.definition: This is a bias that may appear in the output if participants are not familiar with VR systems, potentially leading to incorrect conclusions.

concepts.name: Pre-exposure assessment
concepts.definition: This refers to the assessment conducted before the user is exposed to the system.

concepts.name: Prior experience bias
concepts.definition: This is a type of bias that can be eliminated by arranging a training session.

concepts.name: tangible and intangible reconstruction fidelity item
concepts.definition: This is a specific item used in the study for which scores were collected.

concepts.name: Welch t-test
concepts.definition: This is a specific statistical test used to reveal significant differences between groups of users.

concepts.name: Digital avatar
concepts.definition: The digital avatar is a representation whose closeness to reality is attested by the results obtained from those who had visited the island.

concepts.name: SSQ Questionnaire
concepts.definition: A questionnaire used to measure cyber sickness.

concepts.name: Wilcoxon signed rank test
concepts.definition: A statistical significance test performed to determine if there is a significant difference between pre and post exposure situations.

concepts.name: Pre and post exposure situations
concepts.definition: Situations where data is collected before and after exposure to the system.

concepts.name: Total severity
concepts.definition: A measure of the overall severity of cyber sickness.

concepts.name: Oculomotor
concepts.definition: A specific item related to eye movement effects observed during system usage.

concepts.name: Experiment
concepts.definition: A process that involves conducting, describing, obtaining, processing, and visually representing data to draw inferences and conclusions.

concepts.name: Agile development idea
concepts.definition: This is the practical implementation of interactive system development life cycles that will be discussed in the next part of the lecture.

concepts.name: Functional and non-functional requirements
concepts.definition: These are the types of requirements gathered, which include usability requirements.

concepts.name: Feasibility study
concepts.definition: A stage that requires a feasibility study report.

concepts.name: Empirical study
concepts.definition: An empirical study requires identifying participants, setting up the study, and getting participants' time.

concepts.name: Implementation
concepts.definition: The phase that involves both coding and code testing.

concepts.name: Secondary level
concepts.definition: A systematic, structured way of testing, such as black box or white box testing.

concepts.name: Rigidity
concepts.definition: Rigidity is the characteristic where every stage must be completed before the next stage starts.

concepts.name: Deployment stage
concepts.definition: The deployment stage is reached only after all requirements have been identified, coding is done, and usability testing is complete.

concepts.name: Design document
concepts.definition: A document required during the design phase, covering both interface and code design.

concepts.name: Usability study report
concepts.definition: A report required after testing to assess the usability of the system.

concepts.name: Agile development framework/approach
concepts.definition: It is a method that encourages fast development to ensure quick turnaround of projects that are acceptable to the clients.

concepts.name: Iteration or sprint
concepts.definition: This is the development cycle, typically lasting four to six weeks, which includes requirements, development, testing, and delivery.

concepts.name: Production
concepts.definition: This refers to ongoing support, which roughly refers to deployment and maintenance.

concepts.name: Release
concepts.definition: This stage includes testing, training, documentation, and refers to deployment.

concepts.name: Conceptualization and inception
concepts.definition: These stages roughly refer to both the physical feasibility study as well as requirement gathering.

concepts.name: Prototype-evaluate part
concepts.definition: This is the part of the design-prototype-evaluate cycle that focuses on how to build and evaluate prototypes.

concepts.name: Empirical evaluation
concepts.definition: This is a method used to finally evaluate usability.

concepts.name: User experience optimization
concepts.definition: This is optimization aimed at managing psychophysiological constraints.

concepts.name: Optimized experience
concepts.definition: This refers to psychophysiological experience optimization, which is one perspective on the optimization problem in VR.

concepts.name: Optimized resource utilization
concepts.definition: This refers to technological optimization, which is the second perspective on the optimization problem in VR.

concepts.name: Experience optimization problem
concepts.definition: This is the problem of minimizing cyber sickness or minimizing the possibility of its induction while using a system.

concepts.name: Resource optimization
concepts.definition: This involves building systems to minimize resource requirements while simultaneously trying to minimize cyber sickness.

concepts.name: Experience optimization
concepts.definition: In the context of VR, experience optimization refers to the effort to minimize cyber sickness.

concepts.name: Internal factors
concepts.definition: Internal factors are causes of cyber sickness that are internal to the user.

concepts.name: External factors
concepts.definition: External factors are causes of cyber sickness that are categorized into hardware and VR content.

concepts.name: Virtual locomotion techniques
concepts.definition: These are the techniques used to navigate in the VR world.

concepts.name: User-controlled virtual tours
concepts.definition: A tour in which the user has control over their travel and navigation within the VR environment.

concepts.name: System-controlled tools
concepts.definition: These tools are often an effortless experience with reduced cognitive demands because the system handles the decision-making for the user.

concepts.name: Cognitive demands
concepts.definition: This refers to the mental effort required by the user, which is reduced because they do not have to decide how or where to move.

concepts.name: Lack of user involvement
concepts.definition: This occurs when the user is unable to control the movement, which makes the experience less realistic.

concepts.name: Realistic walking experience
concepts.definition: This is an experience where the user forgets the difference between realistic and unrealistic things, allowing them to feel present in the tool.

concepts.name: System-controlled tour
concepts.definition: This is a tour where the system is forcing the user to move from one place to another.

concepts.name: Enhanced presence
concepts.definition: Enhanced presence is the state of increased realism achieved by improving the walking experience within VR tours.

concepts.name: Model of the user's walking speed
concepts.definition: This is a model that determines how typically a user moves and what the instantaneous speed is during movement.

concepts.name: Psychophysiological optimization
concepts.definition: This optimization is essentially equated with VR experience optimization and aims to minimize cyber sickness prevalence.

concepts.name: Cyber sickness prevalence
concepts.definition: This refers to the condition that we want to minimize while the user is experiencing the immersive system.

concepts.name: VR experience optimization
concepts.definition: This concept is essentially equated with psychophysiological optimization.

concepts.name: Natural walking experience
concepts.definition: This is the goal of having a realistic walking experience within the VR world in a system-controlled tour.

concepts.name: Speed estimation model
concepts.definition: The speed estimation model was proposed using real-life working data gathered from users moving from one point to another.

concepts.name: Photograph-clicking task
concepts.definition: This task was assigned to ensure the user stops after walking a predefined distance.

concepts.name: Instantaneous step frequency
concepts.definition: This is the number of steps per second for the participants.

concepts.name: Data step
concepts.definition: A data step is defined as one foot strike to another foot strike on the ground.

concepts.name: Fourier series
concepts.definition: The Fourier series is a mathematical tool that, with proper weights, can approximate any continuous periodic function to arbitrary precision.

concepts.name: CISO pattern
concepts.definition: The CISO pattern is a pattern observed in the study that was found to be similar to the Fourier series approximation of a square pulse wave.

concepts.name: Perception of visual or optic flow
concepts.definition: Generally, an individual perceives the visual or optic flow slower than the real movement.

concepts.name: Visual gain
concepts.definition: A factor multiplied by the actual speed to obtain a different speed that is perceived as natural.

concepts.name: Actual visual speed
concepts.definition: The different speed obtained by multiplying instantaneous speed by visual gain, which is perceived as natural.

concepts.name: Perceived speed
concepts.definition: The speed at which the scene should change.

concepts.name: Actual speed
concepts.definition: The speed at which the user is moving or the instantaneous step frequency.

concepts.name: User height
concepts.definition: The height of the user, which affects the calculated speed.

concepts.name: Natural walking behavior
concepts.definition: This is the computed natural walking behavior multiplied by a visual gain factor to allow the user to perceive natural walking.

concepts.name: Empirical study
concepts.definition: An empirical study was carried out to confirm whether the usage of the model enhances perceived realism compared to a constant average speed.

concepts.name: Rating scale
concepts.definition: A scale used to measure values, where 1 represents the worst and 10 represents the best.

concepts.name: Realistic walking speed model
concepts.definition: This model is designed to maximize presence and is used in system-controlled virtual reality tools.

concepts.name: CS minimization approach
concepts.definition: This approach is a future topic that rests on the usage of the realistic walking speed model.

concepts.name: Addressing the cyber sickness concern
concepts.definition: This approach involves optimizing cyber sickness by controlling the exposure duration.

concepts.name: Duration of exposure
concepts.definition: The duration of exposure is the time a user spends in the virtual environment, which can be reduced by controlling the speed of movement.

concepts.name: Teleportation-type movement
concepts.definition: This movement involves instantaneous movement between two points, which reduces the overall duration of exposure.

concepts.name: Mental map
concepts.definition: A mental map is a construct whose difficulty in being built can hamper a user's ability to perform wayfinding activities in the virtual world.

concepts.name: System-automated tool
concepts.definition: A system-automated tool is one in which users do not interact.

concepts.name: Semi-interactive tours
concepts.definition: A tour characterized by interaction with Points of Interest (POIs) while navigation is controlled by the system.

concepts.name: Semi-interactive system control tools
concepts.definition: Semi-interactive system control tools are the focus of our objective to reduce the duration of exposure to the virtual world.

concepts.name: Entirely system-controlled VR tool
concepts.definition: A VR tool where the interaction time can be ignored because the system controls all aspects of the experience.

concepts.name: Optimum path (Minimum Time)
concepts.definition: A path that allows users to experience all points of interest while minimizing the total time required for navigation and interaction.

concepts.name: Optimum path (Maximum POIs)
concepts.definition: A path that allows users to interact with the maximum possible number of points of interest within a given fixed time.

concepts.name: Vertex set
concepts.definition: The vertex set (V) represents all the points of interest within the virtual world.

concepts.name: Weighted edge set
concepts.definition: The weighted edge set (E) consists of the weighted edges connecting all the points of interest.

concepts.name: Edge weight
concepts.definition: The edge weight denotes the Euclidean distance between a pair of vertices, or a very large number if they are not directly connected.

concepts.name: Path P
concepts.definition: Path P is the path within the graph that covers all vertices and minimizes the time required while maintaining a realistic speed.

concepts.name: Graph
concepts.definition: A structure where nodes are points of interest, edges are weighted, and the weight is the Euclidean distance between directly connected points of interest.

concepts.name: Actual instantaneous walking speed
concepts.definition: This is the realistic speed of walking, which is related to the perceived instantaneous walking speed by a visual gain.

concepts.name: Perceived instantaneous walking speed
concepts.definition: This is the instantaneous walking speed that is realistic and can be represented by the form 2.1.

concepts.name: Total travel time estimate
concepts.definition: The total travel time estimate ($	au_D$) between a directly connected vertex pair is calculated as $D/V_0$ multiplied by the term $3 - 16/	ext{pi}^2 	imes 	ext{summation}_{k=1}^{N_0} 1/(2k-1)^2$.

concepts.name: Constant Vm
concepts.definition: This is a constant specific to a given height, expressed as 2.1 times h squared divided by 0.157 times 1.72 squared.

concepts.name: Time to travel between two nodes
concepts.definition: This is the problem of finding an algorithm to compute the time required to travel between two nodes directly connected with natural walking speed.

concepts.name: Edge weight or length
concepts.definition: The edge weight or length is the Euclidean distance between a pair of vertices.

concepts.name: Travelling Salesman Problem
concepts.definition: The TSP is a problem that asks for the shortest possible path that visits each node exactly once and returns to the starting node in a complete graph.

concepts.name: Hypothetical edge
concepts.definition: A hypothetical edge is an edge introduced between vertices that have no direct connection for the sake of computation.

concepts.name: Modified edge weight
concepts.definition: The modified edge weight is the weight between two nodes, which is the Euclidean distance if they are directly connected, or the shortest path length if they are not.

concepts.name: Modified graph
concepts.definition: The modified graph is a graph created by introducing hypothetical edges and using a modified set of edge weights.

concepts.name: Complete graph
concepts.definition: A graph created by computing hypothetical edge lengths and replacing the edge set of the original graph so that all vertices are connected.

concepts.name: Shortest path
concepts.definition: The path used to replace hypothetical edges or to determine the distance between vertices when they are not directly connected in the original graph.

concepts.name: Optimal path
concepts.definition: The path that corresponds to the original graph and takes the minimum time to cover.

concepts.name: Minimum time
concepts.definition: The goal of finding a path that covers all points of interest in the shortest possible time.

concepts.name: Cybersickness time threshold
concepts.definition: The maximum time limit beyond which there is a possibility of cybersickness.

concepts.name: Time threshold
concepts.definition: A defined limit on the movement or VR exposure time of the user, above which there is a possibility of cyber sickness.

concepts.name: Optimal path covering maximum number of points of interest
concepts.definition: An approach where the goal is to find a path that covers the maximum number of POIs while adhering to specific time constraints.

concepts.name: Optimal tour
concepts.definition: A path that covers all nodes in minimum time, representing the objective of the previous approach.

concepts.name: Importance of every node
concepts.definition: This term defines how important a specific node is within the system.

concepts.name: Importance function
concepts.definition: This is a function (f, v) that computes or assigns importance to every node, mapping it to a positive real number.

concepts.name: Total importance of a given path
concepts.definition: This is the summation of the individual importance of each node contained within a specific path.

concepts.name: Waiting time
concepts.definition: The time required by the user to inspect or interact with a particular object at a node that is the point of interest.

concepts.name: Waiting time function
concepts.definition: The waiting time function, W, is defined as a function where a node V is mapped to a real positive number.

concepts.name: Total waiting time
concepts.definition: The summation of individual waiting times for all the nodes along a path P.

concepts.name: Importance
concepts.definition: This is the metric that is maximized, and it is defined in terms of the importance of the nodes.

concepts.name: VRP with profit
concepts.definition: This is a generalization of the vehicle routing problem where the goal is to maximize profit within given time constraints.

concepts.name: Vehicle routing problem
concepts.definition: This is a well-known problem that VRP with profit is a generalization of.

concepts.name: Profit
concepts.definition: In this context, profit is defined as being in terms of the importance of the nodes.

concepts.name: POIs
concepts.definition: These are the points of interest (nodes) that the user is trying to visit to maximize importance.

concepts.name: Total exposure time
concepts.definition: The sum of traveling time plus wait time, which must be less than the time threshold.

concepts.name: Optimal path P
concepts.definition: The desired output path where the importance (F) is maximized and the total traveling time plus wait time is less than the threshold.

concepts.name: VRPP solver
concepts.definition: A solver used on the modified graph (G double dash) to process the importance and wait time inputs and determine the optimal path.

concepts.name: Original graph G
concepts.definition: The initial graph structure defined by its vertex set V and edge set E epsilon, along with specified importance (f) and waiting time (w) for each node.

concepts.name: Optimal path formulation
concepts.definition: A method used to find a path that allows the user to cover the maximum number of the most important POIs within a given time threshold.

concepts.name: Psychophysiological or experience optimization in VR
concepts.definition: The objective of this optimization is primarily to take care of cyber sickness related issues or to minimize the possibility of cyber sickness.

concepts.name: Optimal path approach
concepts.definition: This approach involves identifying a path in a virtual world that allows the user to explore all points of interest in minimum time.

concepts.name: Optimal path under time constraint approach
concepts.definition: This approach seeks to cover the maximum number of the most important points of interest within a specified upper limit of time.

concepts.name: Waiting time at a node
concepts.definition: This is a term introduced to help solve the problem of maximizing covered points of interest within a time constraint.

concepts.name: Naamghar
concepts.definition: The Naamghar is the prayer hall, which serves as the central part of the Satra.

concepts.name: Monikut
concepts.definition: The Monikut is the specific place where the idol is kept.

concepts.name: Haatis
concepts.definition: Haatis is the hostel designated for the disciples.

concepts.name: Satradhikar
concepts.definition: The Satradhikar is the master of the Satra.

concepts.name: Euclidean distance
concepts.definition: A distance calculation used to determine the edge weights connecting pairs of nodes.

concepts.name: Maximum wait time
concepts.definition: The estimated time required for a user to stop at a POI, inspect it, interact with it, and then resume navigation.

concepts.name: Contextual inquiry
concepts.definition: A type of field study used to observe people's travel behavior and activities within a specific environment.

concepts.name: Nodes
concepts.definition: The points of interest that are used to represent the campus in the graph model.

concepts.name: Weight
concepts.definition: The weight is the value that serves between nodes or is assigned to an edge.

concepts.name: TSP solver
concepts.definition: A TSP solver is an algorithm used to find an optimal path that covers all the nodes.

concepts.name: Resource optimization
concepts.definition: This is the second type of optimization that is of importance to XR.

concepts.name: VR Resource Optimization
concepts.definition: This refers to learning ways to optimize the resource requirements of Virtual Reality.

concepts.name: Resource Optimization
concepts.definition: This is one of the major types of optimization discussed in the extended reality domain.

concepts.name: Resource (in VR)
concepts.definition: In the context of VR, resource refers to the hardware part, which includes input devices, processing devices, and output devices.

concepts.name: Software part
concepts.definition: The software part includes developmental tools, software development kits, software packages, or application packages.

concepts.name: Manpower
concepts.definition: Manpower refers to staff required for development, deployment, maintenance, and marketing.

concepts.name: Supporting infrastructure
concepts.definition: Supporting infrastructure includes rooms to keep the setup, the hardware setup, supply of electricity, and furniture.

concepts.name: Digital infrastructure
concepts.definition: Digital infrastructure is related to network gears, switches, routers, wires, and servers.

concepts.name: Good experience
concepts.definition: The objective of allowing the client to have a positive experience with affordable hardware resources.

concepts.name: Hardware resources
concepts.definition: The hardware that is optimized only at the client end or at the user end.

concepts.name: Interface
concepts.definition: An interface is what you get to see on a computer screen.

concepts.name: Object
concepts.definition: An object is a geometric shape that can be part of a particular item or part of the interface, such as menus or icons.

concepts.name: Image
concepts.definition: An image comprises geometric shapes, and there is color attached to each shape.

concepts.name: Interaction
concepts.definition: Interaction is the manipulation of images or parts.

concepts.name: Representation
concepts.definition: Representation is the fundamental question of how to represent objects or parts of an image.

concepts.name: Synthesis
